speakeroldname: Hon. Leon Balcer (Acting Secretary of Slate):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am tabling herewith in English and in French the report on patents of invention of the royal commission on patents, copyright and industrial designs.
The royal commission was appointed pursuant to order in council P.C. 1954-852 of June 10, 1954, to inquire into and make recommendations upon the legislation of Canada relating to patents of invention, copyright, trade marks and industrial designs. The commission's report on copyright was tabled in the house in June, 1958, and its report on industrial designs in August, 1958.
Since the present Trade Marks Act, which resulted from approximately five years' study and discussion by a committee of experts in the light of representations from interested organizations and individuals, is relatively new; since the statute appears to have been well received in Canada and abroad; since the commission, in its report on industrial designs, recommended one amendment to the Trade Marks Act on the basis of its recommendations with respect to industrial designs; and since, finally, the commissions's membership and staff have become depleted and it would be impossible for it to undertake an inquiry into trade marks, it was decided that the commission's terms of reference be amended by the deletion of the reference to trade marks. By order in council P.C. 19591340, dated October 16, 1959, the commission's terms of reference were so amended. There will, therefore, be no report on trade marks, and with this report on patents of invention the commission has now completed its assignment. This report on patents is being made available to the press and for sale to the public today.
Since this report contains matters of a highly technical nature, the government does not intend to introduce the necessary legislation to bring a new act into force at the present session. We intend to give to all those who are interested time to study this report and submit their suggestions before introducing appropriate legislation at the next session of this parliament.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
On January 111 announced that the agricultural stabilization board would make an interim payment to producers for eggs marketed during the period January 1 to March 31. I also pointed out that at that time egg marketings were at a relatively high level, and that this interim payment was being made to provide assistance to producers during the period of adjustment.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The national weighted average price lor grade A large eggs during the period January 1 to March 31 was 25.4 cents per dozen, or 7.6 cents below the prescribed national weighted average support price of 33 cents per dozen.
In establishing the exact amount of the deficiency payment, the agricultural stabilization board took into account the fact that the national weighted average price of grade A large eggs during the last quarter of 1959 was slightly below the prescribed price, and will accordingly pay an interim deficiency payment of 8 cents per dozen. This payment will be made for all grade A large and extra large eggs up to a total of 1,000 dozen, marketed in the period January 1 to March 31, 1960, by producers registered with the agricultural stabilization board. Cheques will be mailed to producers as soon as marketing records for this quarter are completed, which is expected to be within the next few days.
During the period January 1 to March 26, 1960, egg marketings were 7 per cent below marketings for the same period in 1959, and for the week ending March 26 marketings were 12 per cent below the same week a year ago.
The reduction in egg marketings is now reflected in improving price levels. Egg marketings are now in a more realistic balance with domestic requirements, and except for seasonal variations prices may be expected to remain at or above the support level. During the week of March 26 the national weighted average price for all grades of eggs in Canada was 34.9 cents per dozen, or 1.9 cents above the support price, as compared to the national weighted average price for the same week a year ago of 31.9 cents when the board was purchasing eggs to support the price.
The deficiency payments of 8 cents per dozen on grade A large eggs, which will be paid to all producers regardless of location, is 0.4 cents per dozen higher than producers in Alberta and Saskatchewan would have received under a regional average basis, and 0.4 cents less than the producers in Manitoba would have received.

Mr. Speaker, I would be the first one to admit that the Minister of Finance is not easy to follow in debate. I was interested to read of a delegation that visited the Prime Minister during the middle of last month, inviting him to a summit meeting of the chiefs of the Six Nations Indian reserves, an invitation which was, by the way, declined. We have had a lot of promises in the past that have never been kept.
But the spokesman said, after an hour with the Prime Minister:
He is a great talker. He can almost make you forget what you came here for.
I think that was about the position of those in the gallery the other night because, next to the Prime Minister, I would certainly give full marks to the Minister of Finance for being this house's greatest illusionist.
We have some sympathy for the Minister of Finance. Admittedly he has had difficult circumstances to contend with, but we would have more sympathy were it not for our feeling that many of the difficult circumstances have been of his own making. I said the other night-and I think a number of other commentators are confirming the view-that the presentation was really a do nothing budget. Someone amended that by saying, "Well, if it was not a do-nothing budget it was then perhaps doing just the same as was done last year." I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is not good enough.
One has to do quite a bit of searching through ore to try to find a bit of sparkle in this budget. I have been prepared to do that, and I have, of course, every desire to approve of some of the good new items, however slender, that appear there. I think most hon. members will approve of the minister's announcement that the double impact of income and estate taxes on pension and annuity rights inherited by widows and others will be avoided.
I remind the minister, of course, that when the new estate tax was being examined in the committee on banking and commerce, sitting when the house was sitting, I stood alone and indicated that the women's organizations of Canada, including the university women and the national council of women, even trust companies and others who were familiar with these matters, urged that this particular amendment be taken care of at that time. I was voted down, of course, by the

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson overwhelming majority of government supporters in that committee. I think too there will be universal approval of the minister's proposal to increase the exemption with respect to medical expenses, for the benefit of those who are faced with abnormally high expenses these days when such expenses admittedly are rising very noticeably.
It was the Winnipeg Free Press, as the minister might imagine, that made the statement last year that it is not realistic to expect an opposition to penetrate all the deceptions of an often deceptive government. I, of course, would not hope to be able to do that today. However, in reading the resolutions over the week end I did notice some items that have not had adequate attention perhaps to date by the taxpayers. I think, for instance, of resolution No. 7 with respect to the sales tax. This is the way that resolution reads:
That portrait photographs of individuals be exempt from sales tax.
I suppose the uninformed may have taken a little glow from the thought that in getting portraits next Christmas they may be able to benefit from what looks like a reduction in tax. Without any explanation, as is usual in these matters, it would appear that this is not a reduction in taxation. Portraits have been exempt from the sales tax. On the contrary, this vehicle is being used to impose new taxation that has not been imposed hitherto. I think this is a very regrettable, back door and sly method of introducing a new tax. I suppose the minister is following the slogan of the popular song; he is simply "emphasizing the positive". But what is actually happening here is that for the first time it seems it is the intention of the minister to impose a tax on developing the films used in our amateur photography, which you and I take to have developed in the ordinary photographer's shop. So I came to the realization that quite contrary-

speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite wrong.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the minister deny that portraits have always been exempt from tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I will deny that there is any suggestion of putting a tax on films that are being developed for people, as the hon. member has indicated.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am glad, we shall watch for developments.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Darkroom tactics.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do know that the minister's colleague the Minister of National


Revenue advised photo developers that it was the intention to impose this tax for the first time, effective in January of this year, without any change by means of a budget resolution but simply relying on what the department thought was permissive power in the present law. They took the matter to the Department of Justice. It is my submission that we have here a clear exemption of one type of portrait photography with the intention of going ahead with the proposal to impose a sales tax for the first time on the ordinary development of films. If I am wrong I will be very pleased to hear so from the minister.
Before we proceed too far with the budget debate, and in view of the fact that in the city of Ottawa the civil service pension plan covers more people than any other such plan elsewhere, I suggest that the effects of income tax resolution No. 12 be considered by taxpayers very carefully. As most of us know, under certain circumstances a person can withdraw from the civil service pension plan and receive a lump sum payment. This provision is utilized particularly by single female employees upon marriage. The intent of the resolution may be simplification for the tax collector, but we must examine very carefully the effect upon the taxpayer himself.
Apart from some of these items, I do not see that it is useful at this stage, or until we come to debate the resolutions, to refer very much to some of the other items because not very many people are interested in cuttlefish, fish bait, pretzels, instant potatoes and the like, which are prominent in the resolutions this year. At another stage I do, of course, propose to examine very carefully the changes in the tariff. For three budgets we have seen the Minister of Finance come before us as he does, warming his coat tails before the glow of his professed virtue in tariff matters, but with each budget that has been presented we know we have had certain complaints from our best customers. I refer to Britain, Italy, Japan and so on. I suggest that again this year these items will require very careful consideration when we have the bill before us amending the Customs Tariff.
When I spoke briefly the other night, Mr. Speaker, there were a lot of oh's and ah's when I made the statement that the Minister of Finance had been 50 per cent wrong in his forecast of the gross national product, because he had made his forecast on the assumption that no increases in prices would be involved. Over the week end I think most of us have seen that this view has been shared by those

with prominent positions in financial journalism. I find that in the April 2 issue the Financial Post had this to say:
Business planners got an unwanted and unexpected surprise this week: 1959's gross national product made only a bare 3.5 per cent gain in volume. At budget time last year, finance minister Fleming had assumed that prices would be stable and a "real" 7 per cent advance would be achieved in the production of goods and services ...
These G.N.P. trends add to the evidence pointing to slower paced growth in 1960.
I hope the Minister of Finance will comment on this as we proceed. I hope the Financial Post is equally right when it goes on to say:
But it's probably all to the good, say most business analysts. The fewer the excesses this year, the milder any subsequent recession.
However, that was not the minister's forecast last year and, as I indicated, it was just 50 per cent out with respect to volume and an assumption of no increases in prices. When we examined the minister's comments the other night we were greatly disappointed with regard to some of the important matters other than finance lightly dealt with that have a great effect upon our economy and' our financial future. There was certainly cavalier treatment with respect to the problem of unemployment. It was certainly brushed under the rug. In the budget of the Minister of Finance we seemed to have quite a departure from the philosophy of the Prime Minister that "no man is going to suffer". There is nothing new for the unemployed. In fact one could hardly find anything more fatuous than this brief reference to unemployment in the minister's statement, as found at page 2670 of Hansard:
I am confident... that employment will rise as the coming of spring opens up new job opportunities and as the economy continues its upward trend.
What a shame.

If that is all that can be expected, if that is all the minister was prepared to tell us in his budget speech about the pressing problem of unemployment, I say it is cavalier treatment indeed. About agriculture there was nothing at all said. The silence was deafening with respect to our agricultural industry. Notwithstanding the fact that the net income of Canadian farmers as reported, last month, has declined 7 per cent in 1959, did the minister make any comment about that very vital industry in his report to the nation the other night? He did not.
Well, Mr. Speaker, at this stage in our proceedings it is always monotonous-it is monotonous to us as it must be to those on
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson the other side-and indeed depressing to recite even a partial list of the broken promises of this administration. I believe those promises were made not with the feeling that they would ever have to be redeemed, but were made in an election campaign simply from the point of view of embarrassment.
I shall refer to some very briefly. There was the promise to reduce expenditures, and then what happened? They were increased. There was the promise to lower taxes, but they were raised; the denunciation of high interest rates, and they were pushed higher; the promise to provincial governments of benefits which the government find afterwards they seemingly cannot concede; the promise to divert trade from the United States and then they concentrate trade more in the single basket; the promise to cure unemployment, and in the year which our financial treasurer says is a prosperous year we find unemployment worse than last year and rising. There was the promise to reorganize and rationalize national defence. Now, there is almost universal agreement across the country that national defence is in an incomprehensible mess.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that in this picture two things have come into focus. It has become abundantly clear that the Prime Minister is, after all, mortal; and second, that the taxpayers' purse is limited. The taxpayers had begun to wonder if the vision was something they could actually afford or was merely an illusion. What are some of the results? We find that the Minister of Finance today is the one being cheered, mostly, as the strong man of the day. The "no person will suffer" philosophy, as I have said, seems to have been jettisoned as being incompatible with the green light that, at some stage, apparently was given to the Minister of Finance to make our finances more sound. Even the government itself now appears to be reaping the whirlwind of the iniquitous promise seed which it sowed in two elections.
At some point last fall-I think this is very interesting-even the Prime Minister seems to have got green around the gills in connection with our financial distress and must have decided on something new because, after all, a change did take place. The Minister of Finance has given us a review of the past year, but it seems to me that the white paper and his report to the house last Thursday night have left out a great portion of the real bases for some of the changes that have taken place.
I want to ask the house to reflect upon the climate, financial and political, across this country last year, particularly in the

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson fall. I have a little review to show just what the thinking was of people not only in this country, of those likely to be biased in favour of the government, but of onlookers outside of the country. What were they saying six months ago? The Economist of London, an outstanding United Kingdom journal, described Canada as in a financial mess.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will the hon.
gentleman read some of the articles from those English papers that came out about six weeks or two months later, and which corrected those erroneous statements?

That was doubtless after the visit by the minister of the United Kingdom, when he said that Canada's finances were as sound as a bell. But it was also after the time that radical changes were made in the direction of our finances in this country.
The Globe and Mail of Toronto has never been particularly unfriendly to this government. Its financial editor, after hearing the speech of the Prime Minister on our financial policy which was delivered to the Lethbridge chamber of commerce, said this:
As to the cause of tight money, this may clearly be attributed to official policy.
The Montreal Star commented as follows:
We wish that someone he would listen to. would tell the Prime Minister that no one cares whether tight money is due to the Liberals, the Conservatives or hurricane Gracie. Very tight money is here.
Tight money is due to a combination of factors for some of which the government has responsibility. Why not tell what government policy is? Mr. Diefenbaker could. Instead we have to go on guessing.
This was the climate of last fall. The money market certainly told the government that something was wrong and not sound as a bell. I think you and I as individuals, if we had found it so difficult to borrow money, certainly would have thought something was wrong with our operations and would be rather concerned. At the beginning of October the president of the investment dealers of Canada had this to say:
The underlying issue is the absence of leadership by the government in monetary matters.
The financial editor of the Montreal Gazette, commenting on that statement by the representative of the investment dealers, said this-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give the date of the quotations?

October 1, 1959 was the date of the first one. Commenting on that statement the following day the financial

editor of the Montreal Gazette, not unfriendly to this government either, said if that statement of the I.D.B. is to be criticized, the criticism is that the statement has not gone far enough.
Within about a week, in this kind of climate -and I am giving only a few illustrations of what was being said about the financial policy of the government-it is true that the Minister of Finance broke a long silence, something which is unusual for him, and made a statement to the Empire club of Toronto. This followed within a few days that famous television broadcast of the Prime Minister when he delved into financial policy and pouted that the banks were to blame for our situation and said that nobody was going to stampede him.
Within a week we certainly did get from the Minister of Finance something quite different and more positive in connection with financial policy. It appeared that at long last the Minister of Finance had been given by his Prime Minister something in the way of a brighter light with respect to financial leadership in the country. We certainly had been in quite a bit of uncertainty previously. I should like to give an illustration of what the House of Commons was told in the previous session by the Minister of Finance as to financial policy, and the kind of muddled explanation that we obtained. As reported at page 3746 of Hansard of May 18, a question was put to the Minister of Finance and these were his words in reply:
If the banks find they have not an ample amount of money to meet the extraordinary demands for credit that are made upon them today as a result of the upsurge in the Canadian economy, then certainly it is not the intention of the Canadian government to inflict on the people of Canada a repetition of the tight money policy of our Liberal predecessors.
Then the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate asked this question: "What are you going to do to stop it?" To that question there was no answer. There was no answer after the adjournment of the house until the minister started in October to make statements as he has been doing, as I said the other night, every month since. What is the policy? Is the policy that the budget is to be balanced at any cost, or is it the policy enunciated previously by the Prime Minister, namely that no person will suffer-presumably economically-in this country?
The Minister of Finance the other night had quite a bit to say about debt management. There was a striking absence of comment on unemployment and agriculture. However, he had a great deal to say about debt management. I think some of the statements made

the other night are certainly worthy of a review. As reported at page 2677 of Hansard the minister said this:
-the total volume of direct government of Canada marketable issues outstanding at the end of the year is only $28 million higher than at the beginning.
What is the unsophisticated person going to think about that statement? I suggest to the Minister of Finance that no matter how he may twist or squirm, all he requires to do is look at the statistics in the weekly report of the Bank of Canada-and I refer to the latest one, dated March 31 of this year- and he will find that the total of government of Canada direct and guaranteed securities outstanding is up $756 million from a year ago. This is the sum that was taken by the government from the market, and taking this sum diminished accordingly the amounts which investors would otherwise have had available for other undertakings, for other governments, for the commerce of the country and so on. I say, Mr. Speaker, what lubricity there is in this kind of statement.
The finance minister's remarks on the debt management activities of the government in the past 12 months just glossed over the tremendous damage that his borrowings have caused to junior governments and to individual commercial borrowers. The course of the treasury bill rates during the year 1959 reflects these repeated demands made by the government on the money market. The Minister of Finance suggests that these rates really, in their rise, reflected particularly the heavy demands that were made by ordinary commerce through the banks. It was the earlier demands of this government for money, made through and after the conversion loan, that demoralized the interest rates of this country and made it no longer possible for the Minister of Finance to say, "look what we as a government have done to bring down interest rates". Once they started to rise, of course, it was somebody else's fault. First of all it was said it was that of the Bank of Canada; then it was said it was the fault of the chartered banks of the land. But the course of the rise is evident. It stemmed and originated from that unfortunate conversion loan.
Give the most recent Bank of Canada rate.

I am going to refer to that matter. I suggest that the hon. member, like the Minister of Finance, may claim credit that it is going down. You are taking great credit for it going down, but refused to accept any responsibility for financial policy when it was going up to heights never experienced in a generation. I want to say something about what this has resulted in. Let us look at what
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson the cost of interest has meant to this government-and we are examining the accounts of our government for the past year-quite irrespective of the calamity that its policies have caused in pushing out other governments and pushing out the legitimate commerce of the land.
The main estimates for 1960-61 provide for interest in a staggering sum, but this is not all the story. The amount of interest actually provided in the book of estimates for the forthcoming year is less than was spent by the government last year. The amount is $594 million. The actual interest charges last year amounted to $632 million. I pointed out the other night that there is an allowance of only $140 million for extra charges for the remainder of this new year if he is actually to produce a balanced budget. The other night he provided $15 million for the civil servants. But here is a difference of $39 million between what was actually spent last year on interest and what is provided for in the estimates for interest for the coming year.
The question that naturally arises is this. Can the minister, with an item of this kind and many others that I could mention, hold the line to this margin of $140 million in the large budget that is involved for this country? We know this government has indicated that as far as freight rates are concerned, an increase cannot be allowed. They have said that the line must be held. Indeed, the president of the Canadian National Railways said to our committee the other day that if freight rates went up he thought there would perhaps be a diminishing return to the railroads. In competition with other carriers the freight carried would become less. We have at the present time a board of conciliation with respect to the wage demands of 100,000 of our railway employees. If freight rates are to be held as they are and subsidies are to be continued in order to provide wage increases commensurate with increases in wages to workers in other segments of the economy, what is that going to do to the budget of the Minister of Finance?
The minister always has a desire to relate the national debt to per capita debt. We are sorry that we have not in the house these days the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan). We hope, however, that he will be back with us after an operation after the Easter recess, at which time he will doubtless be participating in later stages of this debate. But I am surprised the Minister of Finance would repeat this old tale after the excellent way in which it was presented to the house last year, when the hon. member for Welland pointed out that what the minister was really saying was that every baby

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson born and every immigrant arriving into the country is simply being handed and assuming a share of the debt. The member for Welland also pointed out that this does not in any way reduce the debt by one dollar. It is simply a matter of transferring to a new baby a share of the public debt.
The net debt as it stands today is $12.1 billion. The Liberals, so much attacked by the Minister of Finance in the past when he sat in opposition for reaching large surpluses, as a result reduced the net debt over a period of 11 years from $13.4 billion to just over $11 billion. In two years this new administration has managed to wipe out half the savings achieved by their predecessors over a period of 11 years.
The cost of servicing the public debt, as a result of the high interest rates and unprecedented deficits in peacetime, now stands at $786 million. This is the second largest item in our budget, being second only to that for national defence. Let us look at the cost of servicing this debt today per wage earner. If we take the figure for the total labour force as approximately 6,200,000, I calculate that the cost would be $126 per year or about $10.50 per month for each wage earner in this country to service the debt. This, of course, is a tremendous obligation, and it has been rising to great proportions.
Mr. Speaker, in connection with debt management, I want to look at another angle. In examining the Bank of Canada report I have found there set out the details of the various forms of loans obtained last year by this administration. We have features that have never been prominent in requests for money over many years of this country's history. Loan after loan seems to have coupled with it a new gimmick and I suggest something which one would almost regard as a new give-away, so far as the taxpayers are concerned, in order to get money.
I refer to such things as the non-callable feature. We have had non-callable features in our public debt in the past, it is true; but I pointed out in the budget debate last year, when referring to the conversion loan which was made, that it would be a financial tragedy of great magnitude when the youth of this land, when they became taxpayers, found there were no callable features as far as. the government was concerned respecting that massive conversion involving $6.4 billion.
This has continued. In the past there were occasionally times under the previous administration when the callable feature was omitted, but I suggest there is a very big difference between the elimination of a callable feature when interest rates are 3 per cent and 3J per cent and when they are 6J per cent or 5J per cent, at all time high levels.


This is what the Minister of Finance is denying to his successors in the way of financial adjustment in the future if interest rates go down.
I refer to the debate of last year of March 18, when I said there was another very dangerous gimmick which the minister was apparently introducing. That was the gimmick of a very substantial discount offered with respect to a very short term loan. I do not know whether the minister was as naive as he suggested, whether he actually did not realize the implication of this, or whether he was endeavouring to mislead me or put me and the hon. member for Welland off. Also the Leader of the Opposition-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the hon. gentleman wishes to leave that imputation on the record. It is not worthy of him to suggest that an hon. member of this house was endeavouring to mislead him.
I was suggesting an alternative, Mr. Speaker, which I thought the minister perhaps would less like to have, and that was that he did not realize the implication to the crown-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must take objection to the imputation in the words used by the hon. gentleman. He has his opportunity to withdraw that expression, when he suggests I was misleading him.

I withdraw willingly, the words "misleading me," Mr. Speaker, and in doing so I will indicate that if one reads the remarks of the Minister of Finance as they appear in Hansard of March 18 of last year, it will be found that he said in reply to remarks made by the hon. member for Welland, "What difference does the length of the term make?" We had described the value to shrewd, sophisticated investors of getting a substantial discount on the purchase of a government bond and utilizing that, if they were not dealers, as a tax free capital gain. Indeed, one wonders why, if it were not deliberate tailoring, we had what would normally be called a treasury bill which would not be subject to a capital gain advantage, but by tailoring the loan for merely a period of one more month, 13 months, it was called a bond.
I pointed out last year that as a bond this was indeed a very expensive form of floating loans on the part of the Minister of Finance. He did not seem to realize that the discount portion of the loan extending over 12 of the 13 months was worth more to a person or a corporation paying income tax of 50 per cent than was the nominal rate advertised with respect to it across the country, the low and unrealistic

rate advertised at that time being 2f per cent. I said at that time that for a taxpayer who was paying an effective income tax rate of 50 per cent, and who was entitled to a capital gain, it was equivalent to a rate of 6.6 per cent for a bond sold at 100 cents for the dollar. I said in addition that I thought the Minister of Finance was suggesting in this form of procedure, providing short term bonds, a form of finance to the junior governments, and that as the collector of most of the income tax in this country he would regret it very keenly as time went on.
Some of the governments, following the example of course of the Minister of Finance, have been entering into this type of financing to a much bigger extent than ever before, and the sufferer is the treasury of Canada which does not get, on the difference between par and the discounted price, any income tax if the purchaser of the bonds is not a dealer and is thus entitled to have the discount regarded as a capital gain. I think this reached proportions of a dangerous nature. The Minister of Finance did not take that advice, and during the year we had subsequent floatings of loans with this important discount feature over a short term. I say this is going to prove very expensive indeed to the other side of the government, the tax collecting department, when they are seeking to collect income tax.
Then toward the fall we got into something which I think is particularly frightening to the young people of the land, if they just care to look at the type of financing which the minister has embarked upon. I have already said that most of his loan flotations do not give him the right, if interest rates go down substantially in the future, to call the debt, as used to be the practice when interest rates were nothing like as high as these. But here, time after time from September on we have had loan issues which have no call right and another feature called the right to convert. In other words, the sophisticated borrower sees that he has all the benefits of the present high rates of interest for bonds maturing over a short period of time, in 1962, 1963 and 1964, and then if rates of interest prevailing in this country in those years are substantially less he has the right to extend the term of those loans, in some cases up to an additional 13 years.
One can readily recognize this form of finance is certainly going to prove very costly indeed to the taxpayers of tomorrow, who are the youth of today; and this in spite of the fact we have indicated these dangers to the Minister of Finance in the past.
Then we come to Canada savings bonds. Even the Auditor General suggested that 79951-0-182
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson there seemed to be a lot of unnecessary and expensive run-around with respect to this form of finance. Canada savings bonds, when they were introduced by the previous administration, may have had some social benefit. They were tailored to encourage savings on the part of the small individual of the land. The maximum amount under the previous administration available to any individual was set at $5,000. Under the new administration there has developed another sales gimmick. The bonds formerly never available to other than the small man, are now available to estates and trusts. They are available to an amount of $20,000 in the name of any one individual, instead of being available to a total of $5,000. I do not think this can be called a small man's form of lending his savings to the government.
The minister's report shows that in the fiscal year just past he did, it is true, sell $1,455 million worth of Canada savings bonds at extraordinary high rates of interest. But the report also shows, at page 267 of Hansard -and this is also contained in the white paper-that the minister in the same year redeemed $1,170 million of Canada savings bonds. In other words he has just been rolling this debt over, and the net increase in borrowings of this nature was only $285 million during the year as shown by this report.
This has even provoked complaints from provincial treasurers. When it had some social merit, providing a vehicle for lending money in small amounts, as under the previous administration, up to a limit of $5,000, these complaints did not arise; but the minister will have noticed that the treasurer of his own province of Ontario has long since cried "ouch" and "foul" against this practice, and only last week these were the words used in the legislature by the premier of Ontario with respect to this type of federal financing:
I do not agree with what they are doing. I feel it is totally unfair. It is "hot'' money, and the turnover is tremendous.
I have indicated that the minister cannot have this both ways. I suggest to him that he is always criticizing the opposition and saying we are the prophets of doom and gloom. I say to him that the biggest prophet of doom today is the Minister of Finance if he thinks we shall have this tight money situation with us so long that in 1962, 1963 and 1964 he must be prepared to give lenders an option to renew their loans at 1959 and 1960 rates of interest for high interest rates such as are indicated in the Bank of Canada report; for another 13 years, seven years and
2870	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson so on. I say he is the pessimist if he thinks that interest rates at levels such as we are experiencing at the present time are to continue for 13 years or more.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made some comment on the fact that in the last month the rate being paid for treasury bills has fallen very substantially. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that this being so he might get in touch with the commercial arm of the Bank of Canada and see if something could not be done to reduce the rate of interest being charged by the industrial development bank to commercial oorrowers.
This would have a very healthy effect upon business in this country, and would provide a healthy stimulus. In March 1959 this government bank raised its charge to borrowers from 6 per cent to 6J per cent. Last October 1 it increased the rate again from 6| per cent to 7 per cent. I suggest that in view of this drop in the treasury bill rate from about 6 per cent last September to 3.26 per cent on March 30 last, the minister might consider carefully whether business would not be stimulated if borrowers who cannot go into the securities market or whose applications are turned down by the chartered banks were able to obtain a decent rate of interest from the government bank itself.
Now with respect to revenue and taxes, 1 have indicated what were some of the promises made by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister when they sought a mandate from the people of this country. What do the white paper and the speech of the minister the other night indicate? The minister, of course, compared taxes with the gross national product. Well, we all take pride in the growth of Canada, but most of us think that if a man is progressing in his business and taking in more money he should be expected to get out of debt rather than be complacent about staying in debt.
Apart from that, let us look at the following table. I think, as I have said, that the gross national debt is not being reduced but only being spread more widely; that it is being shared by a greater number of newborn babies. I submit that a more realistic table with respect to tax revenues would certainly have reference to the amount of taxes per capita which are being paid.
I should like to submit a table which I have prepared. It shows a comparative statement of revenues. The figures in each case are taken from the budget papers, and the table compares the revenues taken by this administration in respect of ordinary budgetary expenditures and the old age security fund in 1958-59 with the estimate given the


other night for 1960-61. This indicates that the tax revenues per capita in 1958-59 are $269.48 and in 1960-61, $326.72. That is a very substantial increase indeed, and this from an administration led by a gentleman who went up and down Canada saying taxation would be reduced.
I have here a headline taken from the Toronto Globe and Mail shortly after the present Prime Minister was elected to the leadership of his party. It reads, "Diefenbaker charges Liberals are Pickpockets". Now, when the tax take is considered, comparing revenues two years ago with the expectations for the coming year, I wonder what the people of this country will think of that kind of political propaganda. This was a speech made on a program of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation during a free-time period.
Indeed, it was in the same speech that the Prime Minister indicated that the Conservative party would have a commission set up to report on government economies which might be put into effect. It is almost three years since hon. gentlemen opposite took charge of the government, and this commission has yet to be established. We know that any inquiry as extensive as the one proposed would take several years to complete, and I say this is just a further indication of somersaulting with regard to promises made to the Canadian people in 1957 and 1958 elections.
When we come to consider expenditures we find something which is just as revealing. If we look at the budget papers we find the expenditure reported there for the last full year of the Liberal administration, 1956-57. The total, including old age security payments, amounted to $5,228 million. In the year just ended-and I am not taking the figures for the year ahead; that would show an even bigger disparity-in the year which was reported upon the other night by the Minister of Finance, we find that there is a billion dollar difference since this administration has been in office.
One thing which the Minister of Finance reported in his budget this year-and he did it in his budget speech last year-is the well worn claim, as it appears in Hansard on page 2679, to the effect that because of the very careful and exacting scrutiny of departmental estimates it is likely that there will not be the usual amount of government lapses, unspent moneys that are put into the budget.
The minister said exactly the same thing last year, as recorded at page 2413 of Hansard. These are, of course, good illustrations of the minister's usual modesty.

But bearing these remarks in mind and bearing in mind his suggestion that extraordinary scrutiny has been provided while he has been in charge of the Department of Finance, something presumably never equalled by his predecessors, let us examine the public accounts for 1958-59. We find there that the main estimates for 1958-59 indicated statutory expenditures of $1,788 million. But the accounts show that total budgetary expenditures under statutory authorization amounted to $1,970 million. In other words, the reality was worse than the prospect.
But these are statutory items. What unusual, extraordinary control has been proposed with respect to the items the minister sometimes describes as controllable? In other words, they are voted by parliament. In the main and various supplementary estimates submitted to parliament by the minister authority was given to him to spend $3,818 million in 1958-59. The actual expenditures for those same items amounted to only a difference of $424 million. Does anybody think that careful control, as indicated by the minister, was applied if we have lapsings of $424 million and if as he says, under his supervision presiding over treasury board these estimates of expenditures had received care and attention beyond that of any other of his well-known predecessors. I am afraid the minister is going to sprain his shoulder one of these days patting himself on the back. The trouble is, when one examines these lapsings one finds that it is so unnecessary.
At this stage it is very difficult for anybody examining the budget papers which were presented to us the other day to make a complete and accurate calculation to see how well the minister has carried out his boast in the next year 1959-60 with respect to the close control of the estimates so that lapsings would be minimal. However, by the use of the budget papers it is possible to make a calculation in this respect. Out of budgetary expenditures under statutory appropriations of $2,253 million I do admit that it is not readily possible to follow $21.3 million of expenditures, but with respect to the remainder of this large sum of $2,253 million it is possible to relate the expenditures reported in the 1960 white paper back to the book of estimates for 1959-60 which was prepared by the minister. When one does that he finds that it was proposed in the blue book that $2,056 million be spent on statutory items as appropriations for 1959-60. As I say, in both cases, I have deleted miscellaneous items of approximately $21 million. When this is examined we will find-and I think this is of interest when we consider the 79951-0-1824
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson narrow margin upon which the minister is basing his surplus for next year-that there was an increase of $196 million. I have indicated on how narrow a base the margin is for the minister's next year's surplus.
With respect to non-statutory authorizations voted in supply I find that there were lapsings of $288.6 million. When one examines the records of previous years, he finds this does not indicate to him that the minister has been better able to reduce lapsings under non-statutory appropriations and at times overexpenditures under statutory items than his predecessors.
It was rather amusing the other night to find that this was brought forward again by the minister despite this discrepancy, when one looks to the past two years' record. It is reported that the other night the Minister of Finance went up to the press gallery after delivering his budget address. One of the journalists asked him a question. It is reported in this way:
He fenced nimbly with a reporter who asked him if the modest $12 million surplus was over-taxation, a sin for which the one-time opposition critic used to castigate the Liberal government.
"That was different," said Mr. Fleming. ''The Liberals were guilty of inaccurate budgeting."
I have indicated the kind of lapsings and discrepancies between the estimates of the Minister of Finance in each of two years.
I indicated some kinds of promises that remain unfulfilled. In fact, what we are getting now demonstrates leadership diametrically opposite to what was indicated to the electorate would be their policy in the matter of finance.
However, the Minister of Finance last year spoke for the second time in the budget debate, as reported at page 2892 of Hansard of April 21, 1959. This shows the extreme length to which the minister can go in debate in the house. He was dealing with the opposition amendment at that time a year ago, and he said:
I have dealt with the terms of this extraordinary amendment, an amendment which has the temerity to accuse this government of having made promises which it did not make; of having been elected on the basis of promises which it did not give during the election campaign, and of having broken promises which it did not make.
I leave it to the country to decide whether any of the promises I have referred to today are not promises that were made well known across Canada as promises made by hon. members of the administration who now sit on the treasury benches. If that is not enough, let us look at some other promises, promises that related to likely changes in fiscal policy.
There are, of course we have been told, two kinds of promises. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) has indicated

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson that promises made outside the house are not entitled to the same respect and obligation as promises made in the house, and I must confess that some of these promises were made outside the house but by very prominent members of the Conservative party.
Just promises to the people.

Just promises to the
people. We remember that at the national convention at which the present Prime Minister was elected leader of his party they had a resolutions committee. It is true that they did draw up a number of items for the platform for the election that was expected to take place in six months or so afterwards. But after the election of the present Prime Minister as party leader it seems that these platform items were stifled. However, those of use who were here at that time know that no one had a better entree to the goings-on at that convention and to the activities of the Conservative party than that good friend of all of us, Mr. Blakely, representing the Montreal Gazette.
Before these plans in the platform were thrown out we had a report from Mr. Blakely as to the goings-on in the resolutions committee of the Conservative party. In the Montreal Gazette of December 12, 1956 he reported that the party had agreed, through its resolutions committee, on an extension of the housing act to cover existing homes in good condition. We have heard no more about that. It was agreed that they would encourage processing in Canada. What is there in this budget along these lines of fiscal policy. It was indicated that they would encourage national research by a more favourable tax climate. I see the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy): I have no doubt he is still trying to persuade the government to carry out this part of the platform. He probably had a great deal to with getting it in there in the first place. We find that they proposed the development of a deep sea fleet at an estimated cost for 35 ships of some $35 million. That has gone down the drain. Even what we had under the previous administration was sold by this administration.
Sold to Batista.

They promised that they would eliminate the sales tax on purchases by school boards. This is the third budget presented by the minister and we have had nothing with respect to that yet. Then there is another matter which is of great concern to me because I have a bill on the order paper to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act with the same objective that the Conservative party had in 1956, that of providing aid to non-industrial small business through the industrial development bank.

When that bill comes up for consideration I hope that my friends, who in such large numbers form the governing party, will make sure of the passage of the bill.
Here is an amazing one. They proposed that they would withdraw from the taxation field with respect to alcoholic beverages and would leave that field entirely to the provinces. Some credit was given to individual sponsors of resolutions at that convention. The present member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith)-he was not a member then-said that he won his case before the 162 member policy and resolutions committee when he called for an amendment to provide for tax concessions for Canadian oil and gas operators equal to those obtained by United States operators from the United States government. We just heard the other day that the government, after almost three years of responsibility, were finally removing the road block that they themselves created instead of providing a green light for this very important industry in western Canada.
Here is another interesting one. The former member for Gloucester got his way too when he insisted that the word "distinctive" be used to describe the Canadian national flag to be adopted immediately.
We know that these planks in the platform were pigeonholed, but let us look at the matter from another angle.
What about the excise tax on automobiles?

The excise tax on automobiles was another example. In the election campaign the Conservative party made no reference to the promises made at the national convention and in substitution therefor said that they would go by the commitments made to the Canadian people by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), then the party leader. It just happens that many matters having direct reference to fiscal policy were indeed referred to publicly and often by the Prime Minister. In his speech to the Montreal chamber of commerce shortly after his election as leader of the party he said that there would be tax changes if his party was elected to power to put Canadian companies on a basis of equality with foreign corporations or their subsidiaries operating in Canada. After three budgets what have we in the minister's financial proposals with respect to that matter?
Again, in his opening campaign speech in Toroto on April 25, 1957 the present Prime Minister said that there would be less discriminatory methods of taxing Canadian oil companies. This was the plank that the hon. member for Calgary South was instrumental

in selling to the 162-member convention resolutions committee. Again, as reported in the Vancouver Sun of March 10, 1958, the Prime Minister said that there would be drastic changes in the taxation treatment of all companies. He said that under the Income Tax Act further incentives would be provided for Canadians to invest in Canadian equity stocks. That was also in his opening campaign speech at Massey hall, Toronto, on April 25, 1957.
Then we come back to the project of the hon. member for Lambton West. Tax reductions to encourage Canadian research in every field, which was also referred to by the Prime Minister at Massey hall on the same date. At a Conservative rally at Campbell-ton, New Brunswick, on May 4, 1957 the Prime Minister promised tax inducements to persuade business firms to process raw materials in Canada.
As I say, these were promises made to the people of Canada outside the house and I think that most of us are disappointed to find little implementation of these well-known commitments made throughout the country in three budgets presented by the Minister of Finance.
I am not going to deal with this matter at any length. Not only in these monthly speeches of the Minister of Finance to chambers of commerce, empire clubs and others prior to presenting the budget but also in what he said to the House of Commons the other night, in which there was very little change from what he had been saying elsewhere, the minister closed his remarks by urging people, with that ring in his voice, to work and save. Of course, the poor unemployed would like to be able to work so that they could save. In past budget debates time after time the minister has used the Biblical reference about the mote and the beam and the eye. If the minister is trying to tell workers and people generally throughout the country that they should follow a policy of self-reliance and that there should be some forbearance and self-denial, I suggest that the minister simply look at the government telephone book of April, 1957 and the new directory and compare the number of staff for each of the ministers then with the number of personal, political staff now. I think the government is certainly not leading the way in forbearance, self-denial or, indeed, self-reliance.
A 50 per cent increase.

In department after department we find no indication of ministers seeking assistance from the permanent professional staffs of the department but rather
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson the addition of publicists, associate private secretaries, executive assistants, and so on. As somebody has said, the number is almost double what it was in 1957.
So I say that if the administration really desires to follow a policy of economy the ministry would be better advised, if they are not practicing self-reliance, to look to the permanent civil service for advice and counsel and not to political advisers to the extent that a comparison of the two telephone books indicates has taken place, contrary to their professions about economy. I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud):
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the financial policies of the government will produce a fourth consecutive over-all deficit in a year of "so-called prosperity", while at the same time offering no solution to the problem of rising prices, rising trade deficits, a continued high premium on the Canadian dollar, increased pressure on provinces and municipalities to borrow outside Canada, declining farm income, and high and rising unemployment."

I had hoped that the minister would have undertaken some moves to plug the many loopholes existing in our income tax laws at the present time. I had hoped there would, be a review of the extremely generous depletion and depreciation allowances that exist. We all hoped there would be an increase. allowed in the exemptions for the average wage earner in Canada and that the exemption for single people would have been raised at least to $1,500 and for married people to at least $3,000, with a much greater allowance for dependants than exists at the present time.
I had hoped that the government would have given some consideration to the institution of a graduated corporation tax in Canada. I cannot see the logic of applying a graduated income tax to individuals in Canada and yet having a flat percentage rate of corporation income tax. I feel that a graduated corporation tax would serve many useful purposes. It would make it a little bit easier for the small businessman to survive as a small independent businessman. It would be a weapon that would help to discourage the development of monopolies and cartels. It would reduce foreign investments to more reasonable levels. It would encourage the sale of offerings of federal, provincial and municipal governments on the money markets.
We had hoped that the government would at long last have instituted a capital gains tax which would also bring in its wake many helpful solutions to the problems of the Canadian economy. We talked about the difficulties-the premium on the Canadian dollar and investment by people in the United States in Canadian industrial enterprise-and the institution of a capital gains tax would be another method whereby in an orderly and planned manner we could bring about desirable results to the benefit of the future welfare of Canadians.
The minister hardly mentioned the field of agriculture. I suppose in the opinion of the Conservatives agriculture is no longer very important; at least, their action henceforth have not shown that they pay much attention to the needs of agriculture. I would like to ask what has happened to the demand for parity prices, and what has happened to the demand for deficiency payments when goods

are exported? There is no planning in this budget to grant either parity prices on home consumed good's or deficiency payments on exported goods.
Neither is there anything contained in the budget which will bring any measure of hope to what the minister admits is an average figure of 350,000 unemployed persons. May I point out to the minister and the government, in seeking ways and means of adding to its revenues, that if we had 350,000 as an average level of unemployment we thereby lost over $1 billion worth of wealth which would have gone into the Canadian economy. The attitude of the government of the day toward the unemployed of Canada seems callous indeed.
This Conservative government has now introduced the means test in the application of the Unemployment Insurance Act, a most regrettable move. The Unemployment Insurance Act was passed on insurance principles, and the introduction of the means test and the denying to these people of the benefits of their severance and holiday pay is completely opposed to the original intent of the act.
The independent businessman of Canada will receive small comfort from the budget. Ever since the Conservatives took office we have only had one lousy, measly $30,000 vote in all the estimates specifically designed to help the small businessman. How they were going to help the small businessman of Canada before the government was elected. Interest rates are now so high that they are beyond the ability of Canadian enterprise to afford. They are also beyond the reach of those responsible for supplying us with our social needs. Our municipalities, hospital boards and school boards simply are not doing the necessary borrowing because they feel that our home owners, in turn, can no longer pay these high interest rates on such borrowings. Our businessmen, especially our independent businessmen, have ended their major borrowings for the very same reason. They can no longer operate when they have to pay these excessive rates.
The government is deliberately responsible for raising the interest rate, and when one looks back now to the speeches made both by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and by the Prime Minister at the time of the bond conversion deal, he will realize that practically every one of the predictions and forecasts as to the blessings of this deal has since been denied by the facts.
We were assured that this move had to be made in order to rid the market of an excessive supply of short term securities. Yet after the bond conversion deal was completed the government itself simply flooded
The Budget-Mr. Regier the market with its short term securities, and the provinces and municipalities were not helped to market their own securities. There were many other forecasts and predictions made as to the wonderful blessings of this move, and I cannot think of a single prediction made by the minister at that time which he would now be willing to repeat in this house.
The government is responsible for making tight money tighter still. Tight money became tighter because of the desperate moves of the minister in the money market, and the banks of Canada had to bail out the government in order to make the bond conversion deal a success. The weekly statistics released by the Bank of Canada show that the minister's bond conversion deal would have been a flop if the banks had not come to his aid on an emergency basis. Of course, that made tight money tighter still, and the ordinary man just was not able to borrow.
Then the bottom fell out of the bond market, and in the words of one of the heads of the Canadian banks, the banks had to put a sounder foundation under the bond market and around about August of last year again had to come to the aid of the government and increase their holdings of bonds. Because of the interest rates being pushed up, large corporations left the market and went to the chartered banks in order to meet their capital needs. As a result, the small man in Canada has certainly had to take a beating.
The budget indicates no action will be taken to reduce the premium on the Canadian dollar which harms Canadian exporters so much and also works such a hardship on Canadian manufacturers. No action is indicated to increase our exports so that they may be more even with our imports. There is no action taken on behalf of the veterans of Canada so that their relative purchasing power in relation to the average wage earner of Canada can be restored to what it was shortly after the first world war. There is nothing in the budget to give any hope to those of us who look forward to more federal aid for education. Our municipalities certainly have nothing at all to their benefit from this budget.
We see nothing in it which will enhance economic aid or reduce defence spending. We see nothing in the budget which will encourage greater Canadian ownership of Canadian resources. There is nothing in the budget to deal with the serious transportation mess we are getting ourselves into and which will take hundreds of millions of dollars of public money to get us out of so as adequately to serve the needs of the nation. There is nothing in the budget to indicate

The Budget-Mr. Regier any awareness of the serious economic difficulties in the Atlantic areas of Canada. There is nothing in the budget for the masses of the Canadian people.
Our many problems were realized by the Conservative party and the Canadian people at the time of the last election. After three years what do we get? We get a speech from the throne that ignores these matters, and we get a budget which again refuses to recognize our difficulties. The budget contained a little bit for some civil servants. It was a balanced budget and a glowing report. Resolving our problems will take a lot of money. However, the wrong steps have already been taken by this government-inflation and getting more deeply into debt. The Tories have done both these things. The new budget of the Tories is a negative one. The only efforts they have undertaken have resulted in higher taxes, higher tariffs and higher interest rates.
The budget should be balanced by raising the productivity of the Canadian economic scene. We need vastly expanded production and all our people at work. We need more intensified production. Our whole economy is becoming more and more vulnerable to what happens in the United States of America. The glowing reports, when analysed, reveal that our prosperity is very narrowly based indeed and that an ever smaller number of Canadians are being allowed to share in the growing production and prosperity that we are said to have.
Moneylenders and foreign investors are having a field day in Canada. The government is applying the brakes to the development of the Canadian economy, and it is applying the brakes to a rising standard of living for most Canadian people. I appeal to the government to recognize that in this day and age its first responsibility is to the broad mass of the Canadian people. The people expect that their difficulties will be recognized and that action will replace pious appeals, and because we feel that the government, in the budget, is not recognizing its responsibilities to the Canadian people, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West:
That the amendment be amended by striking out the period after the word "unemployment" and adding thereto the following words:
"and in the opinion of this house the solution of these problems requires amongst other things that the government give consideration to the following measures:
1.	The planned elimination of wasteful defence expenditures
2.	The provision of a self-liquidating public investment program
3.	The provision of an appropriate capital gains tax."

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard A. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in what terms might I most appropriately describe the sallies and the sneers which have been launched against the budget this afternoon by opposition spokesmen? Having heard them, I thought that perhaps I should follow the example of the late Humphrey Mitchell, and speak in a kindly way. Is not what we have witnessed this afternoon a parade of the picayune, the piecemeal, the puerile and the perverse?
Have there been any objective, discriminating critiques of the budget, of fiscal or tax policy, or have we heard political harangues and abusive declamations? Have we heard constructive criticism, or churlish captiousness? The house and the country have a right to expect from the opposition's financial critics constructive, realistic, forthright and substantial criticisms. What they have received was a peddling of gloom, of pessimism, of despondency, of dejection. These qualities, however they may be a reflection of the political futures of the parties to which hon. gentlemen opposite belong, do not capture the mood of the Canadian people today and do not represent the reality of Canada's future, of her unprecedented and unparalleled development.
In what he had to say this afternoon about existing fiscal and taxation policies, did the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) propose any alternatives whatever? Did he give the house and the country any concept of the policies he would pursue in the unlikely and unhappy event of his becoming minister of finance? Carefully I listened to him, hoping for some clue. None did I gain, and none was there. With respect, may I say that his speech was in my opinion the most negative I have ever heard from a financial critic.
I am not one who believes that an opposition is under a duty to parade detailed policies on every issue. But I do affirm it has an obligation to assert its principles, to demonstrate on important fiscal matters where its principles and theories differ from those of the government. A hodge-podge of strictures is no alternative to statements of principle.
Presumably, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and others of the front bench of the group opposite-I adopt the word "group" to which they have been demoted by the hon. gentleman who represents Essex East (Mr. Martin)-will be speaking in this debate. Specifically and directly I invite them to state their fiscal principles, their economic tenets. Let them tell us what in this year 1960 would be their tax policy. Do

they believe in a balanced budget at this phase of our economy? What would they do about our deficit on international payments, except to talk about it? Would they stop the inflow of capital abruptly or gradually, completely or partially? Would they join their great expert Walter Gordon, who may become the minister of finance instead of the hon. gentleman from Kenora-Rainy River, and devalue the dollar, whatever that expression means? If it means something which technically it does not-merely reducing the value-how is that to be accomplished? Would foreign exchange control be reinstated? Would hon. gentlemen opposite peg a fixed rate of exchange and, if so, by what technique? Or would they go into the market and engage in a gigantic financial speculation in the purchase of foreign currencies? Have they, in fact, any cure which is not worse than the disease?
These are fair questions which I put to hon. members in the Liberal group. If we are to have an eight-day debate let it be a debate. Let us know where each party stands; let us get to grips with reality; let us thresh out the issues and the principles which are before us.
This amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River gives us no clues concerning Liberal policies. All it does is condemn; it does not assert. It is a warmed over version of the various amendments already proposed by the Liberal party to the address and on supply motions. I say to the hon. gentleman that the repetition of inaccurate assumptions-and that is all this amendment achieves-does not make them any more accurate or more palatable. I think I should add at once that the sophistical and unrealistic subamendment assuredly does not improve the amendment. In fact, I was thinking as I read through the text that both the amendment and the subamendment had obviously been drafted by experts, and I use the term "expert" in the sense in which Nicholas Murray Butler defined it, as one who knows more and more about less and less.
I do not propose at this time to spend any time replying to the speech of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier). That speech reminded me simply of one which Disraeli characterized as "the harebrained chatter of irresponsible frivolity". The hon. gentleman succeeded only in demonstrating one thing, the validity of the epigram of Viscount Hailsham: "The Left can never be Right". If the hon. gentleman is the spokesman of the so-called new and unnamed party of the left, its future might well be that described by a United States
The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell congressman who, speaking of another party, said it was "like a mule, without pride of ancestry or hope of posterity".
How old is that one? Why not say what you think instead of quoting the views of other people?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Not from you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I say to the hon.
member that nothing becomes him so much as silence, and I hope he will observe it for a little while.
Let me deal with some of the matters which have been raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. In his anxiety to score debating points he fell into many grave errors this afternoon. Last Thursday night, and indeed again this afternoon he alleged that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had forecast for the last fiscal year an increase in the gross national product of 7 per cent, and in an imaginary horror he exclaimed that it was only 6 per cent. Let us test the validity of all his strictures by this one. What he forgot to tell the house was that the dominion bureau of statistics, after the last budget, revised upward the 1958 preliminary figure of gross national product, thereby involving a shift in the percentage by which 1959 could exceed it. What the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech of April 9, 1959-and I quote from Hansard at page 2409-was this:
I shall be basing my budgetary policy and my revenue forecasts on a gross national product of about $34) billion which is about 7 per cent above the average level achieved in 1958.
In other words the forecast was a dollar amount of $34J billion. What is the actual figure for 1959? It is $34,593 million, or $93 million more than the forecast figure. I ask this. Has the house ever seen closer estimating in respect of figures so astronomical? The margin of error is fantastically small.
Why, then, this talk of 6 per cent as opposed to 7 per cent? When the Minister of Finance brought down his budget on April 9, 1959 the preliminary estimate of the 1958 gross national product was $32,184 million. On this figure the forecast 1959 gross national product of $34J billion represented an increase of approximately 7 per cent. Later in 1959, the dominion bureau of statistics, on the basis of later information, adjusted the 1958 figure upwards from $32,184 million to $32,606 million, on which of course the percentage relationship was slightly less.
What my hon. friend failed to do was to compare the comparable. If you compare the
