The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell preliminary 1958 figure of $32,184 million with the preliminary 1959 figure of $34,593 million you will find a 7.48 per cent increase.
This increase compares with the post-war average increase of about 4 per cent. In other words, our rate of growth in 1959 was almost double the average of other years since 1945, and this despite the fact that our rate of expansion was subject to a temporary but very significant pause in the third quarter of 1959, due to the effects of some major labour disputes. These are the real facts. But, in one of his scattered jibes on this subject, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River claimed that the Minister of Finance was 50 per cent wrong and he repeated that this afternoon.
In volume.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
My hon. friend was not 50 per cent wrong. He was 100 per cent wrong in this as in so many other subjects that he discussed.
For his forecast of the gross national product, his forecast of the budget deficit and other estimates, when compared with the actual, the Minister of Finance certainly need offer no apology. On the contrary, I believe he can proudly assert the smallest margins of error that there have been in history. Let hon. gentlemen opposite produce examples of any budget of recent Liberal ministers of finance where the forecast was so closely vindicated by actual performance, where the margin of error was less. All of us remember when time after time that very distinguished minister of finance, now Mr. Justice Abbott, would be $300 million and $400 million out in his forecast of budgetary balances. That was budgeting in those days by accident.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River attempted to find something sinister in the technique of dealing with the old age security fund. The Minister of Finance has loaned that fund $24 million, which amount will be repaid out of an anticipated $30 million surplus this year. Oh, said my hon. and genial friend from Kenora-Rainy River, if you had not done this your deficit would be $24 million greater. He cannot have it both ways although he tried to do just that very often this afternoon; he tried to have things both ways many times. Suppose he was right in the assertion which he makes; then, the inevitable concomitant would be that next year's surplus would be $30 million larger than that which has been forecast.
On many occasions this afternoon my hon. friend seemed to take great pleasure in playing with bookkeeping items. With great respect I would suggest to him that this hairsplitting brand of dialectics profits us not at all, and that he really should leave these


tactics to his colleague on the front bench who is an expert therein, namely the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith).
We heard some things this afternoon about unemployment. Not for a moment do I discount the individual problems which are involved. I could not do so, since it perhaps falls to my unfortunate lot to interview more persons seeking employment than perhaps any other hon. member of this house. But in their preachments of gloom, in their wal-lowings in pessimism these Jeremiahs opposite fail to tell us the whole story. It can be found in the white paper. There are more persons employed at better wages than at any time in our history. Total employment rose by 156,000 persons between 1958 and 1959. Labour income reached a record level of $17.7 billion, almost 8 per cent above 1958.. Since consumer prices roses only about 1 per cent, there was a substantial gain in real income.
A few weeks ago the Leader of the Opposition made a very realistic and I thought a surprisingly objective appraisal of some of the causes of unemployment and I think his example might be followed by some of his colleagues on the front bench opposite, particularly the hon. member for Essex East.
In all his declamatory rhetoric this afternoon, in his jibes the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River totally ignored the very substantial fiscal accomplishments of this government, the very genuine advances in fiscal and tax policy. I want to take a few moments to discuss ten of those highlights, adding the caution that this review and listing are not, of course, intended to be exhaustive or exclusive.
First, and at the top of my list, I put the successful financing of the greatest increases in social justice payments ever made in any period. What are the facts? Direct payments to individual Canadians by the federal government for social justice account have increased more than 50 per cent over the last year of Liberal government and that tremendous dollar increase has had to be financed from revenue.
This is all nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My hon. friend could find out if this is so by examining the record.
Will you allow me to deal with that now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that is so. If he would only allow his statistical genius to have full sway he would discover the exact figures.
Would my hon. friend permit me to point out that whatever benefits there are-
Order.
They do not like the truth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My time is limited. My hon. friend's skill in building up men of straw is exceeded only by his volubility and ability to create diversionary tactics. I do not intend to be diverted in this way.
In the last year of Liberal administration old age security payments were $379 million; last year they were $574 million, an increase of about 52 per cent, and this is the story generally across the board.
Second, the fiscal policy of the government provided the incentive for recovery from the recession. In June of 1957 Canada was tottering on the verge of a depression. Had we not reversed some of the policies of our predecessors, recession would have become all-out depression. The reductions in taxes in 1957 and 1958, together with the introduction of many hundreds of million of dollars into housing, transportation and resources development, were designed to augment investment, to stimulate recovery and to provide employment. These policies succeeded.
Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to have forgotten that housing in Canada was coming to a virtual standstill when this government took office. It was the tremendous stimulus given the industry under the imaginative direction of the then minister of public works, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), that saved the day. The flexible and adjustable fiscal policies adopted by this government enabled the country to emerge from recession into recovery and renewed growth, and in the last fiscal period to experience an expansion of major magnitude as well as soundness.
Third, and in due course, has been the achievement of a balanced budget in the forthcoming fiscal year. For sound reasons the Minister of Finance deliberately budgeted for a substantial deficit in 1958 and for a reduced deficit in 1959. Two years ago we were meeting the problems, as I have said, of a recession and were seeking to use fiscal measures to offset the decline in business activity and to stimulate recovery. In 1960 our position is different. Deliberately, in this period of expansion, the government has brought the budget into a surplus position, a position where the federal government ceases to be a net borrower, thus leaving the capital market free to the extent of some $700 million to the provinces and the municipalities and to business and industry. Let
The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell no one think that this has been easily attained. Without the determination, the persistence and the tenacity of the Minister of Finance it could not have been accomplished. This balanced 1960 budget is a personal tribute to the hon. member for Eglinton.
The fourth major accomplishment of the government has been the achievement of relative price stability. No one can ever assert in a dynamic society the conquest of inflation. But we have accomplished an avoidance of disturbing fluctuations upwards or downwards in the general level of prices. In the last fiscal year of Liberal government the consumer price index rose 4.1 per cent. The first broken year of Liberal and Conservative government shows an increase of slightly less. Since that time, in two years the price index has risen 2.9 per cent or an average increase of less than 1.5 per cent a year. I say that ceaseless, unremitting vigilance to control inflationary pressures is essential to our progress, as the Minister of Finance so eloquently mentioned in his budget speech the other night.
Then I come to the fifth matter, the effective management of our public debt. On this matter an uncommon lot of nonsense has been talked, none more so than about the conversion loan, and we heard some of it this afternoon. This was the greatest financial operation in Canada's economic history. It was a major anti-inflationary step, it removed a heavy pressure on the bond market and it nearly doubled the average length of our debt.
Suppose there had been no conversion loan. What would have been the pressures upon the capital market with this heavy debt maturing? If such pressures had been added to the pressures which actually did develop in 1959, the result might well have been chaos. History, I believe, will prove that the conversion loan of 1958 has been one of the most farsighted acts of financial statesmanship ever undertaken.
Last Thursday evening and again this afternoon the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River engaged in some agile dialectics about the net debt. How it has risen, he exclaims. But he really did not tell the whole story in connection with it. It is true, of course, that our total net debt has risen but so has our ability to pay. The fact is that our per capita debt today is $681 as opposed to $849 in 1950 or $701 in 1956, the last full year of Liberal administration. Was the hon. gentleman heard in protest in those earlier years about the size of our per capita debt?

The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell
Equally, what is not clear from what he said this afternoon is that our net debt as a percentage of the gross national product has declined. Back in 1950, in the heyday of Doug. Abbott, our net debt was 71 per cent of our gross national product. When the Liberals went out of power it was 36 per cent. Today it is 34.9 per cent, a lower figure than in any previous year except 1958. The best evidence of effective debt management is, first, that public holdings of dominion of Canada bonds are at the highest level in the last 10 years and, second, that public subscriptions for the last Canada savings bonds were the highest ever. The public of Canada, with their dollars, have voted for the debt management policy of the government.
And the high interest rates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My sixth point is the question of dominion-provincial relations. There have been many things said by way of criticism but overlooked were the most significant and revealing facts. The first is that in the last full year of Liberal government total payments of all kinds to the provinces were $689.4 million. In this fiscal year they will be $1,300.9 million. That is an increase of $611.5 million or about 88 per cent.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My time is very limited, Mr. Speaker.
Then the hon. gentleman will not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Actually unconditional payments have increased by 57 per cent and conditional payments by about 250 per cent.
Most of it Liberal legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
That was the question I was going to ask the hon. gentleman. Tell the truth.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman interrupts like that it reminds me of what Bacon once said, that universities incline wits to sophistry and affectation, and if there ever could be proof of that it is found in the hon. gentleman.
It is in the hon. member's speech.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
Atlantic adjustment grants have been a major contribution of the government. The settlement of the university grants issue with the province of Quebec on a mutually satisfactory


basis is a magnificent contribution to national unity. It is one for which credit must go to our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), to the Minister of Finance, to the late premier and the present premier of the province of Quebec. What an act of constructive statesmanship. Let us give credit where it is due. And have hon. gentlemen opposite forgotten the 50 per cent increase in the amount of the grants? Let them give credit for that.
Who started them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The seventh major contribution of the government is its effective tariff policy. Attempts of a rather childish nature are made to claim that this government is a high protectionist government and has departed from the principles of multilateral trading. Since the government came to power there has been a firm adherence to the principles of the GATT. Indeed, what we have tried to do is to give leadership in GATT, not just pay lip service to it as our predecessors did. We have tried, with success, to use GATT as an instrument in the removal of restrictive trade practices, and this we must continue.
Let those who criticize our tariff policy assess the success of the negotiations regarding fruits and vegetables and textiles. Let our Liberal friends tell us during this debate if they would have ignored the tariff board report on fruits and vegetables. If not, will they not admit our genuine success in concluding these delicate negotiations with the United States? No constituency will profit more by that than the constituency of the hon. member for Essex East.
Before this debate is finished we shall probably hear much on textiles. That the Liberal party will seek to face both ways, I have no doubt. But this house knows and the country knows that the Liberal party wholly ignored the plight of the textile industry. It sold the industry down the river and it has not relented-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What are you doing now?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: -in its callous disregard of a great national industry, one of the largest employers of labour. When the Leader of the Opposition speaks in this debate let him tell us whether he would have accepted or rejected the tariff board reports on textiles. That is a specific and direct question that I put to him, and it should have a direct answer.
When do you want the answer?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When the hon. gentleman speaks. He will have plenty of time.

My hon. friend
does not want an answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I had not discovered that the hon. gentleman had taken over the role of the Leader of the Opposition. I know he has been most un-co-operative with the Leader of the Opposition and has been trying to take it over but I had not realized that he had succeeded.
That is not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The amendments to the Customs Act which were so bitterly fought by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill) and others have been a significant contribution to orderly trade. When he speaks perhaps the Leader of the Opposition would tell us directly whether the Liberal party would repeal them, amend them or retain them.
Coupled with this is my eighth point, namely effective leadership in commonwealth trade policy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my time is limited and I do not feel that I can accept questions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman leaves his point about textiles would he permit me to ask a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Normally I am most happy to answer questions, but my time is exceedingly limited and I am endeavouring to cover a very broad field.
In this area there is a significant difference between hon. gentlemen opposite and this government. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not really believe in commonwealth trade though they give lip service to it. We do believe in it and we do not apologize for this belief. As a direct result of the commonwealth trade conference, sterling and other European currencies have become convertible, a major advance, and the great majority of discriminatory restrictions against dollar imports have been eliminated.
What are the other results? Our contribution to the Colombo plan in southeast Asia was raised 50 per cent. For the first time we sponsored aid programs for the British West Indies and for Africa. This technical and other assistance was and is an act of enlightened leadership. I will admit that these are not the last word in aid to underdeveloped countries. Indeed we are probably but on the threshold. So long as people anywhere in the world are hungry this wealthy nation cannot be complacent. Well
The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell may it be that in this field will lie our greatest contribution to peace and the democratic way of life.
From the conference, as well, flowed the establishment of the commonwealth scholarship plan, a plan which in my view may prove ultimately to be a major beacon light of the 1950's.
I come to my ninth point, the major tax revisions. The replacement of the old dominion succession duty by the new Estate Tax Act was a major advance in tax legislation. But there have been other detailed and significant revisions of our tax structure. Take for example the new provision for a tax free gift of $10,000 between spouses respecting a jointly owned home, or in the case of a farm, between parent and child; the reduced sales tax on a wide range of municipal purchases; the inclusion of drugs, eyeglasses and many other categories in medical exemptions, as well as the raising of the exemption limits in this budget; the reduction in automobile excise tax; the very many tax reforms introduced, including in this budget two very significant proposals, first the relief from the impact of double taxation on pension benefits and, secondly, a new technique of tax deferment on profit sharing plans. Let it not be forgotten that for the lower and middle income groups income tax rates are lower than when this government was elected. The tax position of small corporations has also been greatly improved.
As my tenth point I wish to say a word about civil service matters. Controversy has obscured some of the major facts. Let me set the record straight. It was this government which put into effect the last civil service increase and which had to raise the funds for it. It was this government which proved itself the true friend of all civil servants by managing a change of government with the least upset of any change in Canadian history. There were literally no dismissals. Contrast that with the parade of firings which occurred when the Liberals came into power in 1935. What a scandalous and unconscionable display of political patronage occurred at that time including what Pierre Casgrain did in this very House of Commons, which was the worst of all.
It was this government which in its first year of office provided increases for superannuated civil servants, something which the former government for 10 years refused to do. It is this government which last session fully revised and improved the Defence Service Pension Act, the R.C.M.P. pension provisions and which at this session of parliament proposes a revision of the Public Service Superannuation Act. It is this government

The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell which after Easter will introduce a complete revision and modernization of the Civil Service Act itself, to bring it up to date and to improve and assure for all time the true practice of the merit system.
It is this government which established the pay research bureau which the previous government had declined to do. It was established so that the pay data could be assembled on a scientific basis. This is the atmosphere in which the government at the first feasible opportunity had decided upon a class to class system of pay increases with increases for 50,000 civil servants effective at once and the balance before the end of summer. Oh, yes, I have neglected to mention the medical-surgical plan, one of the major advances in civil service matters.
Representing as I do more civil servants than perhaps any other hon. member of this house I am not unaware of the disappointment which existed at the decision not to approve a general pay increase last autumn. But I am satisfied that a class by class approach will enure in the very near future much more to the benefit of the average civil servant than a horizontal increase. We have seen how horizontal increases in freight rates have merely accentuated the existing discriminations. Continuous horizontal increases in salary perpetuate and intensify discriminations as between classes and help the high ranking civil servants to the detriment of the lower paid. That is why I believe this continuous class by class approach will prove much more effective and much more beneficial to those I represent than would a single horizontal increase. Under this approach, with the pay research bureau in action, review of salaries will be more regular, less discriminatory and more in the interests of the average civil servant. To my civil service friends in Carleton who have maintained a responsible and dignified attitude throughout this salary controversy I say-"give this new approach a real trial these next few months. I do not believe you will be disappointed."
I have taken the time to mention but 10 of the major accomplishments of a fiscal nature of this government but there are many others. If time permitted me to do so I would go on to enumerate them. I say, however, that this is a proud record of fiscal accomplishment. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) may justifiably take genuine satisfaction in the economic leadership they have given this country. The promotion of confidence in Canada's economic future, the encouragement and continuation of our unprecedented economic expansion, a continued

assault upon inflation, the maintenance of a sound dollar, the relief of the capital market thereby easing credit; these have been major objectives of this budget. These objectives have been achieved in the budget for 1960, I believe. In my opinion, in their accomplishment the Minister of Finance has earned the gratitude of the house and the country.
Mr. Speaker, before the hon. gentleman resumes his seat would he permit me a question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I already have, but if I can improve the hon. gentleman's knowledge I will endeavour to answer his question.

I should like to ask the hon. member if he is aware that in his speech he made the same misleading statement about payments to the provinces that the Prime Minister made on television and that has been corrected more than once in this house?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that statement which I made is entirely accurate. It was accurate when previously made and it is accurate now and can be proved by an examination of the white paper.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the amendment introduced earlier this afternoon by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) I wish to say at the outset that I will deal with the main points referred to in the amendment together with the position of the government in relation to the civil servants of this country. I will leave to others the task of replying to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) who just made another of those "What would you do?" speeches which we hear so frequently from hon. members opposite. It is a clear indication that the government still seeks advice from the opposition.
The hon. gentleman reminded me of an auctioneer in the approach he adopted. He could easily have said, "$12 million once, $12 million twice, $12 million three times, gone". That is just about what will happen to the meagre surplus which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) introduced in his budget, a surplus of which the hon. member for Carleton and other hon. members opposite are so proud, one which may be attained at the expense of the civil servants of this country including those residing in the constituency of the hon. member for Carleton. It was on March 27, 1956 that an hon. member of this house is reported, as can be found at page 2647 of Hansard of that day, to have said as follows:
Well, sir, it is in no personal sense that I must say to the Minister of Finance, in referring to the

budget effort on this occasion, that it was unquestionably the worst failure in Canadian history within living memory. In kitchen terms this budget is as dull as dishwater, and it fell as flat as a pancake.
Further on he said this:
Indeed, sir, if this represents the government's idea of a budget it might just as well have been dispensed with entirely.
Those were the words of the hon. member for Eglinton when sitting on the opposition side of the house. I could not resist repeating those same words today because at no time in Canadian history has a budget been introduced which did so little, offered so little and meant so little to the people of this country. It was indeed a "doing nothing" or a "doing just the same as last year" budget.
This is a case in which someone should have called out "dispense" because by avoiding the reading of this budget the Minister of Finance would have been saved from exposing once again the lack of leadership, the lack of policy and, indeed, the evidence of contradiction which has been so outstanding a feature with the government since it took office in June of 1957.
I know that for over one and a half hours on Thursday evening last the government members, the colleagues of the minister, 44 times burst into desk-thumping applause, notwithstanding the stand-pat aspect of the presentation. It would have been advisable for those hon. members to have reserved their enthusiasm, at least when the minister announced the meagre $15 million increase for one-third of the civil service force of this country.
In his hold the line policy announcement when he flatly refused to grant any general salary increase early last fall the Minister of Finance, in an inept and arrogant way, stated that such an increase would seriously upset the budget. In other words, the civil servants of this country were nothing else but the victims of the unrestrained extravagances of the present government. How could they upset a budget which was already badly disrupted? Now, six months later, the same minister comes back with what is being called too little and too late. The applause from government members-which provoked an ear to ear grin on the normally solemn face of the Minister of Finance-could well have been avoided when the minister referred to the degrees of disparity between civil service salary rates and those of private employers and ended up by selecting one third only of the civil service force for nonretroactive increases in salary.
What about the remaining two thirds of the civil service force? What about the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud Police? In his budget speech the minister took great care to say that a review of all other classes in the public service will be carried out by the civil service commission forthwith and that it is expected to be completed before the end of the summer. What he did not say is that he already has in hand a complete report, an exhaustive study, prepared by the civil service commission and presented to him early in 1959. Not only did he refuse to act on the recommendations of the commission but he even refused to make this report public as requested by opposition members in this house.
In a post-budget press interview, the minister allowed himself to be understood to mean that there was a clear obligation in the budget speech to cover the salary levels of the rest of the civil service by the end of the summer. What is the Minister of Finance waiting for? As I have just said, he has on hand a recent civil service commission report on salaries and he is now attempting to cover up once more by delaying tactics which are uncalled for and unacceptable as the procedure is considered to be far too slow to keep up with changing conditions since the last increase was granted in 1957.
I want to make it clear that once again the civil servants are being victimized by the delaying tactics of the Minister of Finance and that the two thirds of the force not included in the present increase are being used to cover up so that it might be possible for the minister to be in a position to announce a balanced budget.
What a contradiction we find there. The minister could just as well have said: taking into consideration the degrees of disparity between civil service salary rates and those of private employers, the treasury board has now approved recommendations from the civil service commission involving the employees of the public service. In saying this, however, the minister would have had to say further: this will involve an increase in expenditure of about $45 million or maybe $50 million during the present fiscal year. But no, the minister could not do this, because he would have missed his meagre surplus of $12 million. He would have missed the desk-thumping applause of his supporters in the house. He would have ended up with a deficit of $25 million or $30 million.
How inconsistent can the minister be when within minutes of the presentation of his budget in a post-budget press conference he makes it rather clear that there was almost no possibility of stopping before the full civil service force was considered by the treasury board on a class by class basis. If this is so, why does the minister refuse to

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud admit now that the 1960-61 fiscal year, as we all well know, will show the fourth consecutive deficit of the present Conservative administration?
In dealing with the civil service increase the minister has been very open to say that there was no leak. In a post-budget press conference he is reported in the Ottawa Journal of April 1 as follows:
"I'll say quite flatly there was no leak" in the federal budget. Finance Minister Fleming told reporters at a post-budget conference last night.
I have here in front of me the Ottawa Journal for March 3. Under the heading "Fleming Replies to C.S." we find the following:
Civil service leaders were pondering the phrase "subject under continuing study"; was it just polite and non-committal acknowledgement of their renewed salaries plea or was it an indication that the government was actually considering a salary adjustment?
Later on the article states:
Replying today, Mr. Fleming wrote that the case the committee had made in its new submission was "largely a reiteration of previous arguments".
And further:
As to any commitments out of a budget priority for salaries, Mr. Fleming reminded the committee that comment on this subject "at this time"-
"At this time" were the minister's own words.
-with the budget under preparation-would be "improper".
Then he concluded his letter with the assurance the salaries question was "a subject under continuing study".
A few weeks later, on March 25, this same newspaper, namely the Ottawa Journal, in an article under the heading "New C.S. Pay Approach to Fleming", reported as follows:
In its announcement of plans for the new approach to the finance minister, the committee dropped a few hints of the points it would try to make with Mr. Fleming.
They included:
1. The finance minister's own "quite emphatic" statement on the last committee interview in October that his hold the line policy on government salaries "was intended for the 1959-60 fiscal year only;-
If this is not enough to let anyone believe that an increase was coming in the present budget, I do not know how it could be otherwise interpreted. It may be well and good for the minister to huddle together a series of wild guesses and figures which, for the time being at least, may temper down the disappointments and frustrations of his fellow members.
Let us look at the facts. Does the present budget come to grips with the economic problems facing the country today? This is a government which is well known for its promises. It has been a government


which has committed itself to defeating the problem of unemployment. "We are defeating the problem", said the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) at Prince Albert on February 14, 1958. At Cornwall ten days later on February 24, the Prime Minister said, "We have acted; we are meeting unemployment. We have given our young Canadians hope. We have given them the vision".
Our young Canadians, as I said before in this house, cannot live on hope and vision alone; they want work and employment. Our unemployed as they stand today deserve better consideration from the government than they are receiving from the present budget.
What were the words of the Minister of Finance in the presentation of his budget when he referred to unemployment? As reported on page 2670 of Hansard, he said:
I am confident, however, that employment will rise as the coming of spring opens up new job opportunities and as the economy continues its upward trend.
Here again is the minister hoping to be saved once more by luck, if ever luck comes his way.
Can we imagine the argument used by the minister when he said that as a result of an unusual increase in the number of persons estimated to be in the labour force, the estimate of the number without jobs and seeking work was 18,000 higher than a year ago? What would this increase in unemployment be today if the immigration influx into this country would have followed its normal course? The coming of spring, not government policy, will open new job opportunities, says the minister. This, at last, is a frank admission by the Minister of Finance himself of the lack of policy, lack of leadership, lack of planning by the present government. As our leader stated the other day in a "Nation's Business" broadcast, this government hopes that unemployment will go with the snow. It had better start moving fast, because the snow is pretty well gone, especially in the vicinity of Ottawa, but the number of unemployed is still rising. In fact, there were 814,241 live claims for unemployment insurance benefits as of February 29, and 827,512 unplaced applicants as of March 10 of this year. And while the economy continues its upward trend, according to the minister, the number of unemployed is increasing day by day and the government is hoping for spring to rush its course and come to its rescue. More sun, more rain, more mild weather, less snow, more jobs, hopes the Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Finance has refused to recognize the urgent need to give direction to

the economy of this country. His attitude is typical of the present government's complacency; it is based on hope, on the hope that everything will come out right in the end. The gross national product, says the minister, will again increase by 6 per cent and on this assumption he believes that the unemployment problem will adjust itself accordingly. He seems to forget, however, that notwithstanding a 6 per cent increase in 1959 the number of unemployed at mid-February of this year had reached 8.9 per cent of the labour force against 8.8 per cent at the same date last year. It has adjusted itself, but in reverse. The snow is going down but unemployment is still going up.
This government refuses to meet the challenge of unemployment and chooses to stand pat on the tired assumption that everything will come right some day. It is a government without leadership, without definite policy. It is a government which in less than three years of office has already lost the overwhelming confidence with which it had been entrusted by the electors of this country. Here again let us listen to the minister. As reported on page 2670 of Hansard, he said:
The past year was notable for a welcome absence of speculative excesses in production, demand and inventories. I stress this because often in the past such excesses have provided a major cause of recession.
In other words, is the minister taking satisfaction in the fact that the 1958 and 1959 crop years were so much below the previous recent years that excesses or surpluses of inventories in wheat and other grains have been cut down? Is he taking satisfaction from the fact that the 1959 net income of farm operators is estimated at 7 per cent below the previous year's level? Is he welcoming the fact that as at December 31, 1959 storage holdings of fish products were over 63 million pounds as compared with holdings of 56 million pounds on December 31, 1958 and 52 million pounds on December 31, 1957? I sincerely hope that the minister is not welcoming the excess in the inventory of unemployed, which under the present administration has reached records unequalled in this country since the hungry thirties.
At the present rate of unemployment the Minister of Finance will soon be called upon to supply additional funds to the Department of Labour to secure or replenish the unemployment insurance fund, which since this government took office has been depleted by over $504 million. At the present rate of decline the entire fund will be practically exhausted, wiped out, by March 31, 1962.
The sum of $383 million standing to the credit of the unemployment insurance fund as at March 31 is a figure to be concerned
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud about. We are asking now, what does the government expect to do about this? Does it expect to save the situation by this discriminating position it has adopted toward the family employment or toward its unjust and unwarranted treatment in its determination of the insurability of relatives? Does it expect to save this fund by attempting to destroy this family relationship and family unity which is traditional among our French Canadian and French Acadian large families? Some of the recent decisions of the unemployment insurance commission in this regard are nothing else but unfortunate attempts to undermine this family unity and good understanding.
Very little was said in the present budget having to do with the records of the present administration. The records I have in mind are not the kind of records which one should be too proud of and which could draw the applause of hon. members opposite. A record debt increase of over $1 billion in two years is nothing to boast about on the part of a government who has committed itself to cut all unnecessary expenses and extravagances.
A record balance of payment trade deficit of $1,460 million in one year is other evidence of the failure to keep up with the Prime Minister's statement made at Brantford on February 17, 1958 when he said that the Conservative government's success in its trade promotion cannot be challenged. The 1959 record of the government shows success in reverse.
What about this other record where the government refuses to take any responsibility? Where is the mention in this budget about this crippling tight money and high interest rates? It is true that the minister has stated, as reported on page 2670, that in the financial sector 1959 was marked by some disturbances which, he says, subsided by the end of the year. What about interest rates on mortgage loans, which again have reached an all time high and have been crippling home construction in the last few months? It is true that the rate of interest of the Bank of Canada has declined somewhat. Does the government intend to take credit for that? If it does, are hon. gentlemen opposite going to take credit for the interest charged to municipalities or for interest rates charged on mortgages? When things are good, the government is responsible, but when things are going wrong, the government has nothing to do with it.
I would ask the minister: what is there for municipalities in this budget? The minister has ignored the plight of the municipalities in this country. I ask him, how can

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud he justify the statement he made at St. Hyacinthe on February 23, 1958, when he said:
We have eased the burdens of the municipal governments by bringing about easier credit and lower interest rates?
How can the minister justify the statement he made at Montmagny on September 28, 1958 when he said that the provinces and municipalities in their financial operations will derive much benefits from the conversion operation? The facts are here to show how far from the truth the minister could be in his assertions. Was it not the Prime Minister who said in Saskatoon, on May 27, 1957:
The Conservative government, if elected, would remove the crushing burden of municipal taxes.
Was it not the Prime Minister who said on May 20, 1957:
The tight money policy has struck a death blow to small business. They are going into bankruptcy at the fastest rate since depression; and municipalities have their back to the wall, forced to borrow money in the United States at high interest rates.
I would ask the Prime Minister these questions: when have bankruptcy rates been higher than in the last two years? When have municipal interest rates been higher than in the last two years? When have municipal taxes been higher than in the last two years? When have interest rates on borrowings for home building been higher than at the present time? When, finally, has a federal government done so little and accomplished so little in facing a problem which, according to the Prime Minister's own admission, was stultifying every part, every section of Canada.
Moreover, what is there in this budget to provide for the $100 million additional requested by Premier Frost of Ontario, a sum which we know the Minister of Finance will be asked to produce at the July federal-provincial conference on fiscal matters? What is there in this budget to provide for additional assistance which will be requested by Premier Roblin of Manitoba, when he will insist that Ottawa change its stand toward the provinces.
What is there in this stand-pat budget for the Atlantic provinces? What is there to indicate any measure of relief for the people of the maritimes who need, not restrictions but more credit and monetary expansion? What is there in the present budget which could even lead to an incentive to accelerate business in that particular area and bring about speedier maximum use of its natural wealth, thereby raising the standard of prosperity in that part of Canada?
Have the Atlantic provinces been forgotten because someone has dared call this budget


a "no-tax budget"? What a fallacy. How can one be so blind as not to realize that the Minister of Finance expects the present tax structure to yield $5,892 million, an increase of $591 million over and above the year before, and more than $1,120 million over and above the fiscal year 1958-59? In other words, the taxpayers of this country will be contributing to the federal treasury over $1 billion more than they were two years ago; over $3 million a day more than they were two years ago. Yet the present government, with all this extra cash at its disposal, cannot find one simple measure which could contribute to narrowing the gap which exists in the income of the people of the Atlantic provinces compared with those of other Canadians.
This, stand-pat, do-nothing budget offers absolutely nothing which could influence the establishment of secondary industries in the Atlantic provinces. The disability of the Atlantic provinces with regard to transportation remains as the main problem, the major obstruction which must be removed if our area is to share equally in the progress and prosperity which in the last decade or so have been so prevalent in other parts of the country. We have a right to know what this government intends to do about the various suggestions which we from time to time have offered in order to stimulate industry in the Atlantic provinces. What does the government intend to do about the idea of a capital grants program and the fiscal incentives which have been suggested both inside and outside this house for some time? Urgent consideration should be given to these proposals. Meanwhile, a solution to our transportation problems, or even the improvement of our transportation system could contribute to stimulating the growth of our secondary industry.
Might I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask when you would find it convenient, Mr. Speaker, to hear a submission with respect to the amendment? I think I am bound to take the view that it is not in order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think that might be done at the conclusion of the speech of the hon. member who now has the floor. That would be shortly after eight o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

When the house took recess at six o'clock I was referring to the numerous suggestions which had been made

from this side of the house to stimulate industry in the Atlantic provinces. I was saying that urgent consideration should be given to our proposals affecting the Atlantic provinces which, if implemented, would contribute to stimulating the growth of our secondary industry.
I deplore the fact that the present budget fails to recognize the plea of the Atlantic provinces. I deplore the fact also that when suggestions are made which could contribute toward raising the level of our economic activity, someone should come right out in the open and launch a controversy which has the effect of spilling cold water on the projects involved. Such controversial statements as have originated recently from Halifax, Charlottetown and Fredericton, involving the Chignecto canal and the Prince Edward Island causeway are most unwarranted and unworthy of anyone having at heart the task-and it should be a national task-of applying national policies for the common good and welfare of all Canadians.
Instead of amending the Excise Tax Act to remove sales tax on electric heating equipment to make it more competitive with maritime coal; instead of including the sales tax on materials used in the construction of ships over ten tons net registered tonnage, the minister could well have listened more favourably to the representations of the fisheries council of Canada on behalf of the fishing industry. The minor exemptions asked for by the fisheries council would have had very little effect on the over-all position of the present budget, but would have been of some assistance to the industry and to a large number of individual fishermen.
Not one single new measure has been introduced by the present government to help the fishing industry which is so vital to the economy of the maritimes. Canada cannot afford to allow the Atlantic fisheries to glide along as if it was to be abandoned to its own fate. There is an urgent need for a definite national plan and policy for the development of our Atlantic fisheries, and wide-scale government attention should be directed to the field of production. The present system of subsidies on the construction of vessels of the dragger and long-liner type is antiquated, outmoded and does not serve any more the purpose for which it was introduced.
Competition in the marketing of our fisheries products is getting keener and stiffer from year to year and this competition originates in countries which are exploiting our own fishing areas along our Atlantic coast. Our fishermen need protection to safeguard their rights and to maintain their source of
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud production. Our fishing industry needs protection to compete favourably with European countries in the traditional markets, and more so when we know that these European nations are subsidizing their own fishing industry. I intend to say more on this aspect of the fishing industry when the estimates of the Department of Fisheries are before this house for discussion.
Notwithstanding the admission by the present government that this country is now out of the recession and experiencing a period of boom, no one can deny that the serious unemployment situation, which is more evident since this government took office than at any time in Canadian history, is causing grave concern and disquietude among the labour class of our country.
The 820,000 unemployed want an explanation from the Prime Minister. They want to hear more about his promise to take the necessary steps to ease unemployment in addition to his billion dollar public works plan. They want to remind the Prime Minister today of his pledge to every man and woman in this nation who is unemployed, "So long as I am Prime Minister no one will be allowed to suffer in this nation." Was he then the leader of the Conservative party attempting to stultify the people of Canada in making such statements, just as he is trying to fool them today in his "Nation's Business" television appearances?
The Minister of Finance should tell us why in this period of high unemployment approved and urgent public works projects have been shelved and put aside for future consideration. Is this policy in line with the Prime Minister's promise that:
As long as I am Prime Minister, no man or woman is going to suffer from unemployment so long as public works will provide them the assistance they require.
Why delay-as is being done in my own constituency of Gloucester-the construction of public wharves which will provide facilities for fishermen, increase their production and supply additional shore help? Why cut down this year's public works projects by the amount of $31 million? In the harbour and engineering branch alone Nova Scotia is cut down by $2.5 million and New Brunswick by almost $3 million. The construction of a number of projects is economically justified. It would raise the economic level of many fishing communities and, as I have just said, it would increase production and provide additional shore help, thus cutting down on unemployment.
The population of Gloucester county learned with interest a few weeks ago that Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud and Sogemines Limited have reached agreement in principle for bringing into production Brunswick's lead-zinc property in the Bathurst area. An initial operation of 2,000 tons of ore a day is good and welcome news for the people of New Brunswick and particularly for the population of Gloucester county. The unfortunate part of it is that those concentrates will be sold to a group of Belgian base metal smelters and again a primary product, a raw material, will be exported to be processed outside of this country. This is not what the people of New Brunswick expected when the mining discoveries of the Bathurst area made history in the mining world in 1952 and 1953. This is not what the Prime Minister promised at Campbellton, New Brunswick, as was referred to this afternoon by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River.
The least that could now be expected from the present government is the provision of adequate port facilities to allow shipments of the concentrates from the port of Bathurst at a distance of fewer than 20 miles from Brunswick's deposits. Such facilities would involve the construction of a spur line from the mine to Bathurst harbour, together with adequate loading accommodation and proper deep water channels to allow easy access for ocean-going ships. Such facilities must not be delayed indefinitely, and if Brunswick's mine is going to operate, as we are assured it is, the government should take the necessary steps now to provide proper planning in order to avoid any possible delay which could in any way jeopardize operation.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the minister that the people of Canada are not being fooled by the additional medical expense deduction which he has offered. We all know that last year-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I tender you at this time my submission that the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidick-son) is not in order. An examination of the amendment itself will serve to emphasize the omnibus nature thereof. While it may be very inviting at times to tender omnibus amendments there are certain risks that are then taken, and in this particular case I think the hon. gentleman has taken risks that have the effect of making his amendment out of order.
May I draw your attention to the breadth of the subjects mentioned in the amendment.
This house regrets that the financial policies of the government will produce a fourth consecutive
tMr. Kobichaud.]

over-all deficit in a year of "so-called prosperity", while at the same time offering no solution to the problem-
Here we have this succession of matters cited.
-of rising prices, rising trade deficits, a continued high premium on the Canadian dollar, increased pressure on provinces and municipalities to borrow outside Canada, declining farm income, and high and rising unemployment.
There we have seven items mentioned. The rule, which I think is quite clear in this respect, is set forth in Beauchesne, fourth edition, page 126, citation 148. The first section reads as follows:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members that they cannot revive a debate already concluded; and it would be little use in preventing the same question from being offered twice in the same session if, without being offered, its merits might be discussed again and again.
The second and third clauses of the citation serve to emphasize the strength of the rule, Mr. Speaker. I think it is the course of decision in the house that two principles have been firmly established in the interpretation of this rule. The first is that it is the substance and not the mere form of the motion, amendment or resolution to which the Speaker has regard in applying this rule. In the second place, if the motion, amendment or resolution offends this rule in part, then the entire motion, amendment or resolution is out of order.
In my submission, Mr. Speaker, while some of the matters enumerated in the omnibus amendment have not been decided by the house at the present session, there are at least several which have, and even one of these would be quite enough to make the amendment out of order having regard to this rule, for if it were possible to support an amendment because part of it had not previously been the subject of a decision of the house in the same session then it would be a simple matter to defeat the rule by simply adding matters which had not yet been the subject of decision.
May I recall to your mind the several decisions the house has made earlier in the present session in relation to some of the matters mentioned in the omnibus amendment. On January 18 the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) introduced the following amendment on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is to be found on page 24 of Votes and Proceedings:
This house is of the opinion that the failure of the government to develop and enunciate clear and consistent policies or to provide full and accurate information, is a major cause of the confusion and uncertainty that prevails about national defence, public finance, agriculture, markets, employment and in other important areas of governmental responsibility.

You will see, Mr. Speaker, that several of the matters mentioned in the omnibus amendment had already been introduced by way of an amendment that sought to condemn the government in the same sense as the present amendment seeks to condemn the government. The amendment to the amendment introduced on January 20 simply added certain words to that amendment. They are to be found at page 34 of the Votes and Proceedings of the session.
Then on February 22 an amendment was introduced on a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply. On this occasion the amendment was introduced by the same hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. It is to be found at page 182 of Votes and Proceedings. It sought to strike out certain words and to substitute the following:
This house is of the opinion that the government should give immediate consideration to the implementation of agricultural policies designed for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment, and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy, thus to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income.
The amendment to the amendment moved the same day by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) purported to add certain words to that. In all of these cases the house resolved the question in the negative.
Again on March 21, on a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply, the Leader of the Opposition introduced an amendment that was intended to strike out certain words and substitute the following:
This house expresses its grave concern at the deterioration in Canada's trading position as emphasized by an unfavourable balance of nearly $1.5 billion in Canada's total trade in 1959, and urges the government to deal with this serious problem by taking effective action, including the working out of proposals for the establishment on a gradual and progressive basis of an Atlantic free trade area.
On the same day an amendment to the amendment was introduced by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) by which he sought to add certain words to the amendment in relation to trade contracts, export credit insurance, planned reduction of foreign investments in Canada so as to reduce the premium on our currency presently handicapping our export industry, greater economic aid to underdeveloped countries, and an expanded and intensified effort by the Department of Trade and Commerce to encourage orders for our goods in world markets.
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I ask where that last one is found?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This last one is also to be found on page 296 of the Votes and Proceedings of the present session. It was an amendment to the amendment introduced on March 21.
I think it is quite clear, Mr. Speaker, from a reference to these amendments, all of which were negatived in the house and therefore are the subject of firm decision by the house at the present session, that a number of the matters included in the omnibus condemnation of the government in the present amendment have already been the subject of decisions by the house at the present session.
I mentioned the matter of the recent trade deficit. That clearly was the subject of the amendment on March 21. The premium on the Canadian dollar was the subject matter in part of the subamendment of March 21. Declining farm income was exhaustively dealt with by the amendment of February 22. High and rising unemployment was the subject matter in part of the amendment of January 18. Therefore I think it is quite clear that the amendment does offend the rule.
I emphasize again that it is the substance of the matter that counts and not mere form. I presume that hon. gentlemen opposite will say that you do not find the matter spelled out in exactly the same words in these earlier amendments which were the subjects of decisions of the house at the session. That is not necessary. That is not the rule. The rule is not so confined. It is the substance of the matter that counts and the fact is that the house has dealt in substance on these various occasions with four of the matters that are included in this omnibus amendment that has been submitted to the house this afternoon.
If it were open to hon. members to introduce amendments of this kind there would be no finality whatever to any decision of the house in a session. It would be relatively simple for any hon. member by exercising just a little bit of ingenuity and merely by changing a phrase or two to invite the house to debate the same matter over and over again.
I think with great respect that this is a situation that has been brought about by the hon. member including too many subjects in the scope of the amendment by which he seeks to condemn government policy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the hon. member speaks may I indicate to him that I see a problem with respect to a couple of the items, as I perhaps indicated when the amendment

The Budget-Mr. Rohichaud was first presented. Since then I happened to have been looking at the previous motions which have been decided by the house and I find that there is substance to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) says. I am particularly concerned about two of the items enumerated in the second part of the amendment, that is rising trade deficits which were the subject of supply motion No. 3 and declining farm income which was the subject of supply motion No. 1. Of course, if these items have been dealt with the whole amendment would fall apart unless the hon. member were prepared to withdraw the defective items.
I just mention that before the hon. member replies to the minister so that he will have that possibility in mind. Those two were the items which appeared to me to perhaps have been dealt with, although there is something to be said too about the question of the premium on the Canadian dollar having been discussed but I think that subject has not been dealt with so fully as the other two.

Mr. Speaker, following your remarks, I think perhaps at this stage it is possible to confine one's attention to the two subjects where you yourself said you have some thought that there may be a duplication of debate that is contrary to our rules.
I too, of course, have reviewed each of the motions to which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has referred. I would suggest to Your Honour that the minister is perfectly correct when he says it is not mere form but substance that we have here. I suggest to Your Honour that the substance of this amendment to the budget is contained in the opening phrase:
This house regrets that the financial policies-
Those are the financial policies, of course, as presented to us by the minister in the resolution which he asked this house to adopt in adopting his budget and it is with respect to the financial policies as outlined in the budget that I suggest to Your Honour we should consider the matter of rising trade deficits. With respect to agriculture the phrase, as Your Honour has indicated, is "declining farm income".
May I first of all say just a word with respect to declining farm income. Irrespective of my point that each of these topics relates to the absence of an adequate policy in the budget I wish to suggest to Your Honour that with respect to declining farm income in particular I can see very little similarity between the phrasing we have before us in
[Mr. Speaker.!

this amendment and the discussion on the supply motion of February 22. I think perhaps Your Honour will surely agree that both the amendment and the subamendment were designed so specifically that we were considering there the cost-price squeeze. We were, in the subamendment, dealing very specifically with what was particularly concerning the agricultural community at that time, namely the situation confronting the producers of hogs and eggs. I would say that the amendment which regrets that the financial policies as presented in this budget fail to deal with the question of declining farm income can scarcely be related to the supply motion of February 22.
With respect to the matter of rising trade deficits, the supply motion of March 21 did, of course, refer to a deterioration in balance of payments but surely the substance of this motion is that we have not in the budget proposals and policies that deal with these matters.
Your Honour has doubtless also reviewed the decision of Mr. Speaker Beaudoin on May 3, 1955 as recorded at page 3425 of Hansard. The then private hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), as has been done today, moved an amendment to the budget. On May 3 after, indeed, we were ready to take a vote Mr. Speaker Beaudoin had this to say:
Considering the fact that on the budget wide latitude is always given, and that the main reason the amendment could have been declared out of order was the fact that the amendments to the address in reply had covered a variety of subjects, I decided not to intervene.
I suggest that that is still valid. Our discussions of the items in this amendment relate to the absence of policies in the financial presentation of the budget itself and having reference to the substance of the amendment and not to some mere technicality of form they do not offend against the rule to which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has referred.
Citation 330 to which the Minister of Finance has referred in Beauchesne's third edition at page 134-and this is on the other point-reads as follows:
When a member hands a motion to the Speaker after having spoken in support of it, the Speaker may, before putting the question to the house, make such corrections as are necessary or advisable in order that it should conform with the usages of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the point of order raised by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and to your remarks. Members of this group are convinced that on two or three points there is some lapse on the part of the mover of the

amendment for the official opposition under the rules of the house. This is a surprising matter in view of their having had the opportunity of securing constitutional, legal and procedural advice and in view of the great experience of the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill).
Speaking on behalf of the hon. members behind me may I say this. Should you find the amendment out of order, in view of this rather incredible error on the part of the official opposition I think that the knowledge of the rules displayed by the C.C.F. should be rewarded by your giving consideration to our subamendment then becoming the amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I appreciate what has been said to assist in dealing with this matter in order to assure that we observe the rules and practices of the house. In addition to the references given to me on both sides, I refer to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 234 which reads in part as follows:
234. The ancient doctrine that the redress of grievances should be considered before the grant of supplies is maintained in the House of Commons of Canada
(1) Whenever an order of the day has been read for the house to resolve itself into the committee of supply or the committee of ways and means-
That is what we are doing now.
-the motion "That the Speaker do now leave the Chair" must be proposed, except on Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays as provided by standing orders 56 and 58. When such motion is proposed, it shall be permissible to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament or to ask for the redress of any grievance; provided that the discussion shall not relate to any decision of the house during the current session, nor to any item of the estimates, nor to any resolution to be proposed to the committee of ways and means, nor to any matter placed on or whereof notice has been given in the order paper.
These four categories which are mentioned are excluded in order to avoid duplication of debate and waste of the time of the house in repeating a debate. It is true that we have dealt specifically, in the first and third supply amendments, with two of these matters. To say that they may now be discussed again in their aspects as subjects of financial policy, which is only one aspect of any problem, would be to permit the house to revive debates of which it has already disposed.
I had practically come to the conclusion before returning the house-and I am reinforced in it by the argument made by the minister and by what has been said elsewhere-that at least two of these items should be removed. In accordance with the authority of the Chair, as mentioned by the hon member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), I think I might direct that two of the 79951-0-183
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud specified items be deleted from the resolution, namely rising trade deficits and declining farm income. Those are two specific items among the seven. I am in some doubt about another one, namely the high premium on the Canadian dollar. However, in view of the broad range of this debate, in any event, and the fact that the former motion on that item was somewhat limited, I think justice would be done and that the time of the house would be saved by avoiding unnecessary debate or duplication of debate if those two items were removed. Perhaps the hon. member who moved the motion would concur in the deletion of those two items.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I be heard on that point, Mr. Speaker? With great respect may I say this. I do not think the rule read by the hon. member concerning the correction of mistakes applies to a matter which vitiates an entire amendment of this kind. With great respect, I submit that power applies only to the correction of mistakes in minor matters such as clerical errors and that sort of thing. With great respect I submit that it does not apply in order to cure in an amendment a clear defect that makes it out of order. If this amendment is out of order in part under the provisions of the rule which I read then it is clearly out of order in its entirety. I therefore submit with great respect, Mr. Speaker, that the power to correct mistakes has no application here. I submit that the proper course is that the amendment be ruled out of order and that it be left to whoever chooses to do so to bring in an amendment that is in keeping with the rules of the house.

I wonder whether I could say a word on the point which has just been raised by the Minister of Finance. I am sure Your Honour will recall previous occasions when, with the leave of the house and in circumstances of this kind, precisely the course that Your Honour has now suggested was taken by the house. My friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has indicated to me that he would be quite agreeable to the course that has been suggested.
However, if I might be permitted just to make this observation with the greatest possible respect, we feel that it would surely never be intended that in a budget debate, notwithstanding the fact that there had been a motion on a related topic, it would not be competent for either side of the house to discuss trade deficits and that it would not be competent for the house to discuss the declining farm income, both of which were discussed by the Minister of Finance himself in his budget speech. It seemed to us that anything that was debatable on the budget, so

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud long as our motion dealt entirely and exclusively with the minister's statement-as we believe this one does; it refers to financial policy-it would be in order. Perhaps we should have said "as set out in the budget speech", but it says that the statement the minister made the other day offers no solution to these problems. Since that statement was made only subsequent to the decision of the house on these other matters, it seemed to us that there was in fact no duplication.

The Minister of Finance has taken objection to Your Honour's following the procedure of directing that the defects in the amendment be corrected. He has done so on the ground that the citation to which reference has been made had to do only with minor defects such as typographical errors et cetera. I think what we need at this time is a little bit of common sense applied to our proceedings. If the Minister of Finance objects and if Your Honour agrees with the minister's objections, I believe the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River would be quite willing to agree to the motion being amended in the way it has been suggested. On many occasions in the past, over a period of many years, when an amendment has been brought in which in general was in order but some parts of which, in the opinion of the Speaker of the day, were in error, those errors have been corrected at the time on the suggestion of the Speaker.
I should also like to make a further point which is a practical one. Since the official opposition has the right to bring in an amendment, a want of confidence motion and since we in this group have the same right or, if it is our only opportunity or alternative, to bring in a subamendment, I think we might just as well have the amendment settled now as wait until some other hon. member of the official opposition speaks and brings it in at that time.
As seconder of the motion, Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed to make a few observations?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that it is unnecessary for him to do so in view of the course which I propose to take. This matter, of course, is a point of order which arose when the motion was made. If I had dealt with it then and if I had disposed of it at that time, it would have been open to the hon. member who had the floor to concur in the suggestion for an alteration, which I have now made at this rather later date instead of then in view of my having made the reservation at the time the motion was just presented. Particularly


as the hon. member who moved the motion and the seconder of it concur in the deletion of two of the seven items, which items I think might be taken as illustrative of the criticism of the financial policies but which nevertheless open the door for debates we have had, I feel that the proper course now is to direct that they be deleted from the amendment and that it stand with that change. It does not affect, then, the subamendment. I am not sure whether the Minister of Finance has any comment to make on the amendment to the amendment which was also reserved, if I am not mistaken, at the time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, do I take it from your ruling that you claim the power to do that, in the absence of consent in this matter? I wish to make it quite clear that there is no consent, and I submit with great respect that in a situation of this kind the Chair has no power to make an amendment or to direct an amendment even if there is consent on the part of the mover and seconder. We have here an amendment which is out of order in part, and under the rules, therefore, it is quite clear it is out of order in its entirety.
With very great respect there cannot be on the part of the Chair any curing of the error in the amendment, the vice which makes it out of order. With great respect, the only course open to the Chair is to rule the amendment out of order. As I said before, the power to cure mistakes is not a power that authorizes the Chair to cure defects, defects which of themselves are so serious as to make an amendment out of order. This is not a matter at all of correcting a word here or a word there which is obviously a mistake. This is something which goes to the very root and substance of this amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I appreciate the force of what the minister says and undoubtedly it is true that, without the consent of the house, a motion which has been put and which is in possession of the house cannot very well be changed. But I take the view that this matter is not in the possession of the house because I reserved it when it was moved, and I now direct before it is put that it be amended and that those deletions be made in the motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on that point, the amendment surely is in the

possession of the house. Once an amendment is introduced and read and then handed to the Chair, surely at that point, it being in possession of the house, it is not possible to deal with it in an ex parte manner. It is an amendment which belongs to the house, and being out of order there is no power to cure a defect in it which is as basic as the defect in this amendment.
Mr. Speaker, if I might be permitted, I might say that you have made a ruling and we respect it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is true I have expressed my view, but I do not want to force my views upon the house unless they commend themselves fully to the house. With respect to the last statement of the minister, I may be mistaken about my authority in this matter, but as I see it this motion was not in the possession of the house because when I read it I said I had doubts about some of these items on the very ground which the minister has taken and that I would reserve them and deal with them before the motion was formally put. The motion being in that state, I think it can be distinguished from one where the unanimous consent of the house would be necessary. Furthermore, the proposed course commends itself to me as one which will further the general interests of the debate. Accordingly I make that amendment with the concurrence of the mover and seconder, and I now put the motion before the house in its amended form.
Before proceeding, the amendment to the amendment was also dealt with in the same way by the Chair at the time, and if any hon. member wishes to say anything about the subamendment this would be the appropriate time. Otherwise I will consider it as having been disposed of at this time as well.

Mr. Speaker, will you clarify one point of the ruling you have made. When does an amendment come into the possession of the house? You say that you reserved judgment on the amendment, so when does it come into the possession of the house? Is it just before a division or when is it?
