Mr. Speaker, it has been said of the budget speech made Thursday night by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that it was a do-nothing, stand-pat budget. It was a neat way of saying that, on Thursday, March 31, 1960, Canada was in the position of a hard-pressed debtor offering its creditors a legal settlement and a moratorium.
During the last three years, the national debt has increased by more than a billion dollars. The unemployment insurance fund has decreased by more that $500 million. To finance its deficits, the government has drawn upon the savings of the people and in order to make its loans more attractive, it has raised the interest to such a point that the savings in our banks, which were used for the development of industry, of business and by the general public, are exhausted through the government's deficits. In this budget, there is no decrease in expenditures and the taxes which had been increased last year remain at the same level, while the rickety surplus expected for 1960-61 is based not only on a hope, but also on the theory that the national product will increase by 6 per cent in the next 12 months.
This budget was evidently devised by a government which as a result of its shortcomings and of its monetary and fiscal errors, has been placed at the mercy of financiers. This budget speech which the Minister of Finance read Thursday night for the public at large is as cold as a tombstone. It lacks humanity and, for the hundreds of thousands of Canadian families affected by unemployment, it is cruel and inhuman.

The Budget-Mr. Deschatelets
In fact there is not even the slightest reference in it to the most important domestic problem in Canada today, unemployment, as if the problem did not exist. To the provinces, which bear a substantial part of the consequences of the government's monetary and fiscal failure, the budget offers nothing that they did not have last year. They will have to fend for themselves. The municipalities which were recently claimed to be heavily in debt, whose taxes on real estate are at their highest level, will have to solve their problems alone; and next winter, I am sure, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) will again ask them to bear the same costs of the winter works program. The government trusts to Providence to take care of the 827,000 unemployed.
If I refer to page 2670 of Hansard of March 31, I find that the only consolation offered to the unemployed are these few lines, dedicated to them, in the tone of a prayer at the end of a sermon.
I am confident-
-said the Minister of Finance-
-however, that employment will rise as the coming of spring opens up new job opportunities and as the economy continues its upward trend.
That sentence, coming at a time when there are more than 827,000 unemployed in Canada, confirms what we already knew, that this government, in its stubbornness, continues to consider unemployment as seasonal and does not care a rap about it. From that angle, the budget of last Thursday evening is an insult to the unemployed of this country.
In the course of my remarks, I intend to make a brief outline of the unemployment problem and of the hypocritical attitude of the Conservative government towards it. But, before going any further, let us glance at the statistics of previous years, under the Liberal regime.
As recorded on page 1654 of Hansard, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) gave a complete statistical table of unemployment in Canada from 1946 to 1959. His conclusions were as follows:
If that table is carefully examined, it will be seen that from the period 1946 to 1956-10 years- the average annual percentage of the labour force without jobs in Canada was 2.8 per cent.
As everyone knows-
The experts in the field say that 3 per cent of the labour force without jobs is the equivalent of full employment.
Well, that magnificent result is not accidental. The Liberals did not trust to spring, as did the Minister of Finance, to provide jobs for our labour force.


In 1945, to ease the change from a wartime to a peacetime economy, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, then minister of reconstruction and supply, tabled in the house what we call a white paper, outlining an eight point concrete program concerning income and employment in Canada for a given period.
If such a program was necessary, at the time, how much more would it be today, when unemployment has reached its highest level since the Conservative depression of 1930-1935?
On March 10, 1960, in fact, the latest figures we had at our disposal showed, according to the national employment service, that 827,512 persons looking for jobs were registered in our offices, and according to the dominion bureau of statistics, there were
555.000	unemployed.
According to the information I gathered,
620.000	persons would now be getting unemployment insurance benefits, after having registered at the end of January 1960.
After personal investigation and research, I am able to say that at present about a third of the above-mentioned unemployed are not registered in our unemployment insurance offices, which would add 200,000 more unemployed to the first group.
If we consider that most unemployed have dependents, it is safe to say that at this very moment, over a million Canadian citizens are suffering from unemployment in Canada. Over a million Canadians are undernourished, over a million Canadians cannot get the drugs they need to restore their health, and thousands of young people, boys and girls, are unable to go on to college because their father, the head of the family, cannot afford to pay for their tuition.
Generally speaking, these people do not share in Canada's high standard of living, which we all like to boast about. Every day, as hon. members may read in their papers, youths of 17, 18 and 20 tell magistrates that they have robbed because they were unemployed and could not find' a job.
In other words, unemployment is not only an economic matter, it is also a social problem. Through the fault of the government, we condone the fact that, in our midst, an imposing group of fellow-citizens are undernourished, that women and children are forgotten, neglected, rejected and deceived by the Conservative party, whose members were

mainly elected because of a formal and solemn promise of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), to the effect that, as long as he would be Prime Minister, nobody in Canada would suffer unemployment, whether there be a deficit or not.
Now, on the evening of March 31, it was time to carry out that promise, but the unemployed were in fact forgotten, and this government, and more particularly the Minister of Finance, preferred financiers to the unemployed.
Now, let us look at the Conservative record with regard to the unemployment question. First of all, there is the Prime Minister's responsibility. After promising so much, he became silent and as the unemployment figures rose from month to month, he became more and more silent.
In the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister and his cabinet undertook on January 15 to give a seasonal character to unemployment, whereas there were at the time at least 700,000 people without jobs.
In early March 1960, we discussed the unemployment question, for eight days, on an item providing for winter works. If I am not mistaken, the Prime Minister did not in that instance come down from his ivory tower. He remained silent.
In the face of growing unemployment, we submitted on March 1, 1960, as shown on page 1578 of Hansard, an amendment recommending "That the problem of unemployment be recommitted to the standing committee on industrial relations".
As soon as the amendment was moved, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) jumped to his feet with the fourth edition of Beauchesne in his hands, trying to discover fine points of procedure by which the amendment could be rejected.
Following rejection of the amendment, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) rose to direct a very plain question to the Prime Minister. May I quote from page 1582 of Hansard the conclusion of the question put by the Leader of the Opposition:
-I ask the Prime Minister whether he will not forget technicalities and ask the house to give unanimous consent in order that this matter may be debated as- a question of urgency by this particular committee.
And here is what the Prime Minister replied, as recorded on page 1582 of Hansard:
I do not really know what the hon. gentlemen means when he says this matter should be debated as a matter of urgency.
The Budget-Mr. Deschatelets
Mr. Speaker, this was on March 1, 1960, and the Prime Minister ended his reply as follows:
-if in that time they have not been able to produce anything, I see no benefit in the suggestion which is now put forward.
And now, perhaps we could put a few questions to the Prime Minister. What is he doing and what has he done about his election promise? Why has he refused to take part even once in the only debate we have had on unemployment in the course of this session? Why did he, on March 31 last, sell Canada's unemployed down the river. And why has he made no provisions for them in the budget, as he had promised to do?
Why did the Prime Minister refuse, on March 1 last, to refer the matter of unemployment to the industrial relations committee?
On February 15, 1954, the Prime Minister, who was then the private member for Prince Albert, made this statement, as recorded on page 2102 of Hansard:
A committee set up to study and report on unemployment would hear evidence of those who are warning this government and the country of the need for action now.
At that time, in 1954, we had only half as many unemployed as we have today.
Mr. Speaker, I leave it to Canada's people to draw the obvious conclusions. I do suggest, however, that after that solemn pledge made in March 1958, the arrogant and unyielding attitude of the government towards the unemployed is one of the most revolting about-faces ever recorded in Canada's political history.
Let us now turn to the responsibility of the Minister of Labour. I should like to recall two statements he made on unemployment, the first one on March 3, 1955, when he was sitting in the opposition. I quote from page 1693 of Hansard:
I think we are wasting time by quoting figures. What is needed is some drastic action on the part of the government rather than the quoting of any figures.
During the period of time that this unemployment situation has gradually increased, no visible effort has been made by the government to alleviate the condition or to provide safeguards against its increase. Consequently we find ourselves with unemployment on a scale of national emergency-
Mr. Speaker, I would remind hon. members who are now listening to me that the unemployment statistics were much less serious in 1955 than they are now. Now, if in 1955 the present Minister of Labour believed that it was a case of national emergency,

On March 3, 1955, as recorded on page 1694 of Hansard of that date, the present Minister of Labour also made this other suggestion:

I ask him now why he did not then mention the number of unemployed, according to the statistics provided by our two official sources.

present time 100,000 unemployed are receiving unemployment insurance benefits in that province. Almost one third of the total number of unemployed in this country are in Quebec.
And the Prime Minister is still silent, the Minister of Labour has adopted a do-nothing attitude, while the Minister of Finance is hoping that spring will bring a solution to the problem.
When we think of this budget speech which ignores the problem of unemployment across the country and, consequently, in the province of Quebec; when we think that that budget speech was received with loud applause by all the Conservative members, including those from the province of Quebec, I say, Mr. Speaker, that I would hate to be in the boots of my hon. friends when the time comes for them to go to the people of the province of Quebec who will call upon them to account for their actions and their solemn promises.

Mr. Speaker,
may my first words be to compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) upon the outstanding budget he produced last Thursday evening. To me it was very reassuring, as I know it must have been to many Canadians, to know that the minister was able to bring down a balanced budget optimistic enough for a small surplus without creating any major tax changes. I should like to commend the minister for making a considerable number of tariff changes, especially those pertaining to cottons as our cotton industry has long been suffering from importations from low wage countries.
This is a budget that seems to be accepted by the opposition parties very reluctantly, for so far they have found very little in it to criticize. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) the other evening and again this afternoon in his feeble attempt to criticize the budget mentioned that the government had a record expenditure, record taxation and record unemployment. I am sure he must have been ashamed of his colleagues when they apparently gloated and applauded as loudly as they did the other evening when he mentioned the high unemployment in this country.

The Budget-Mr. McBain
After listening to the last two speakers I wonder whether we are now debating the budget or are we back on the unemployment debate that we had some weeks ago? Commenting on this budget there was an editorial which appeared in the St. Thomas Times-Journal on Saturday last, April 2, which expresses the thoughts and feelings of a very large number of people across the length and breadth of Canada. The editorial is entitled "A Balanced Budget" and I now wish to quote from it. It begins with these words:
Blessed are they that expect not for they shall not be disappointed.
That probably represents the feelings of the people of Canada in regard to the budget brought down in the House of Commons Thursday night. Reports emanating from Ottawa throughout the past financial year have indicated that although the national economy was improving, no tax concessions could be expected. If hopes are to be entertained for next year much may depend on what happens at Geneva or some other city in regard to disarmament, nuclear agreements and the pacifist attitude in general, for the military part of the budget takes up one third of the expenditure.
However, the country is in a prosperous condition. The general output of production increased and continues to increase, but our prosperity is not sufficient to justify a tax reduction that would really be felt. There are hopes for next March.
The most interesting part of the budget is that the textile industry is to receive increased tariff protection against imported fabrics, and that the tariff board will examine the tariff structure on engineering and architects' plans, nails, china and glass imported for decoration, and mining and petroleum machinery.
The textile industry has been crying out for a long time; way back into the St. Laurent administrations, but then they mostly cried in vain. Factories have been shut or put on short time and textiles have probably contributed more to unemployment than any other business.
On the whole, not a bad budget under the circumstances. I
I think that editorial speaks for most of the people in Canada.
I wish now to discuss some problems that are relevant to southern and southwestern Ontario and portions of Quebec. I wish to refer to the tobacco industry from the production standpoint to the manufacturing process. My remarks will have reference mainly to flue-cured tobacco.
The production of flue-cured tobacco and its processing into a consumer product is an industry on which a great majority of the people in the tobacco growing districts depend for their livelihood. It is also the main support of numerous local industries and services which manufacture, sell or service materials and machines for the tobacco industry. Merchants, garages, service stations, banks, legal firms, insurance and real estate companies and other businesses have gained much from the tobacco industry. It is also the largest customer of the companion branches of agriculture in these same districts.


The tobacco industry may also be found to be the largest single source of tax revenue, if not in the country at least in many municipalities.
Tobacco is the hub of a great wheel of local industry which finds its earnings rising and falling according to the state of the tobacco industry. The general overhead for an Ontario flue-cured tobacco farm exceeds that of almost any other agricultural commodity. At the present time the province of Ontario has approximately 4,500 qualified farms growing flue-cured tobacco in 16 counties. The estimated capital invested in these farms approaches $300 million or an average of between $65,000 and $70,000 per farm. The farm buildings and equipment required to cultivate and cure tobacco cost upward of $40,000 depending on the size of the unit.
The outstanding cost in producing tobacco is the annual labour account. To harvest and prepare this annual crop for market requires up to 60,000 persons and their earnings paid by farmers amount to approximately $45 million. Much of this money is borrowed from the banks at fairly high interest rates. When you take into account the interest on the capital invested, the maintenance and depreciation on farm buildings and equipment together with the high labour costs and the money which farmers borrow annually from the banks, this makes tobacco one of the most costly agricultural crops to produce. An average production cost per acre under present conditions would be $650. This cost is dependent upon the producer being permitted to market his full basic acreage production. Practically all the tobacco farms are equipped to operate to full capacity and when they have to drop back to anything less their production costs per acre increase.
The amount of tobacco marketed each year in Ontario is set by the Ontario flue-cured tobacco growers marketing board before the beginning of the planting season and many factors have to be considered before acreage quotas are determined. The chief factor is not to set quotas at a level that would produce a serious surplus thus depressing prices to a point where producers could not repay their loans made from the banks to grow their crops. At the same time the board must take into consideration the dangers of producing too small a crop resulting in a great demand and a high price and loss of export trade.
The Ontario flue-cured tobacco marketing board is one agricultural marketing association that deserves a great deal of credit because besides negotiating with the buyers to establish a price they also maintain strict controls over their acreage production. In the year 1958 production was very high with a yield of

173,213,818 pounds of tobacco returning an average price of 47.57 cents per pound which brought to the producers $82,394,702.
To market this large 1958 crop the marketing board experienced serious difficulties so that the base acreage for 1959 was reduced by 25 per cent. This the board estimated would yield from 145 million to 150 million pounds. When the sale of the 1959 crop wound up on March 11, 145,220,668 pounds were sold bringing to the producers a gross return of $81,525,841 at an average price of 56.25 cents per pound. This indicates how closely the output was estimated. Despite this extra large return the gross return was some $750,000 less than for the large 1958 crop.
Although this agricultural product is restricted to areas where it can be grown the federal treasury collects more fax in proportion from tobacco than from any other product manufactured. At present a package of 20 cigarettes has a tax of 20 cents or one cent per cigarette; in other words, 209 per cent of the manufacturer's selling price. In Canada the average per capita cigarette consumption per annum is 1,949. For taxation purposes this means a revenue of $19.49 per person. For a family using two packages a day under our present tax they would pay $146 per year. Breaking this taxation down further, I might say that the treasury collects an estimated $3,200 from every acre of tobacco grown. In 1957 when this government came into office, the sugar beet industry and growers were gradually being forced out of business and production. The Liberal government would always say no to a support price on sugar beets, and without a support price and import controls sugar beet acreage in Ontario had dropped from a high of 40,000 acres to
14.000	acres and one sugar beet processing plant was forced to close.
After the change of government in 1957, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his cabinet listened with an open ear to the producers' problems and eventually established a floor price under sugar beets. Since this floor price was implemented the acreage has increased from the low of 14,000 acres, in a two-year period, to 35,000 acres in 1959.
As Canada produces less than 25 per cent of her sugar requirements it appears to me to be a great opportunity to have this agricultural production of beets expanded not only in Ontario but in western Canada as well. I would suggest the government should consider the implementation of a long range sugar policy for Canada. At the present time I am informed that the price of Cuban refined sugar in Cuba is from $2.80 to $2.85 per hundred pounds. As the government of Cuba has a monopoly on sugar and as a result of its present instability I can foresee Cuba endeavouring to dump into Canada refined sugar at a price below the cost of production. If this should happen it would spell ruin for the sugar refinery in Toronto and the beet plants at Chatham and Wallaceburg.
If a long range policy could be brought into effect so that the producers would know where they are going I am sure it would be possible to increase acreage up to a possible 50,000 or
60.000	acres. It would take out of production acres that are now producing crops that at times create a surplus. It would also keep in circulation the $20 million that is now spent for growing, harvesting and processing the sugar beets. It would also create a need for a new sugar beet factory to be built and therefore would give employment to a large work force in construction operations and maintenance.

The present two plants at Wallaceburg and Chatham when operating at full capacity employ 1,500 people. The riding of Elgin which I represent produces a fairly substantial acreage of beets at the present time. If the producers could be assured of a long range return plus import quotas I am sure this acreage would definitely be increased.
In the riding of Elgin we have an excellent location for a new sugar beet factory at Port Stanley. As a sugar beet processing pflant requires a large amount of water for washing and processing the beets, a new plant situated at Port Stanley on lake Erie would have available all the water necessary. Furthermore, the farmers in this area are the producers of a large quantity of the flue-cured tobacco grown in Ontario. When this crop is harvested, usually about September 15, the surplus labour could be diverted to the harvesting and processing of sugar beets.
I wish to commend the government for the steps they have taken in the past to restore the sugar beet industry in Canada. I hope they will continue their interest and will continue to assist the sugar beet producers in 1960.
I think it is gratifying to see the optimism shown in this chamber by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill). In this venture he was extremely successful for he would stand out by the side of his stand and, although unable to read or write, he would spiel out the words "Come and buy a hot dog". It had its effect on the travelling public for Tony's Place became very favourably known far and wide. Tony was successful enough to put aside enough money to send his son to college.
After a year in college his son came home and said, "Dad, how is business?" His father replied, "Business is booming better than ever". "That is strange," said the son; "did you not know there is a depression on in Canada?" His father said, "No; I was not aware of it. I have no television, no radio and, as you know, I cannot read the papers; so as far as I am concerned business is as good as ever". subsubtopic: TABLING OF REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am tabling herewith in English and in French the report on patents of invention of the royal commission on patents, copyright and industrial designs.
The royal commission was appointed pursuant to order in council P.C. 1954-852 of June 10, 1954, to inquire into and make recommendations upon the legislation of Canada relating to patents of invention, copyright, trade marks and industrial designs. The commission's report on copyright was tabled in the house in June, 1958, and its report on industrial designs in August, 1958.
Since the present Trade Marks Act, which resulted from approximately five years' study and discussion by a committee of experts in the light of representations from interested organizations and individuals, is relatively new; since the statute appears to have been well received in Canada and abroad; since the commission, in its report on industrial designs, recommended one amendment to the Trade Marks Act on the basis of its recommendations with respect to industrial designs; and since, finally, the commissions's membership and staff have become depleted and it would be impossible for it to undertake an inquiry into trade marks, it was decided that the commission's terms of reference be amended by the deletion of the reference to trade marks. By order in council P.C. 19591340, dated October 16, 1959, the commission's terms of reference were so amended. There will, therefore, be no report on trade marks, and with this report on patents of invention the commission has now completed its assignment. This report on patents is being made available to the press and for sale to the public today.
Since this report contains matters of a highly technical nature, the government does not intend to introduce the necessary legislation to bring a new act into force at the present session. We intend to give to all those who are interested time to study this report and submit their suggestions before introducing appropriate legislation at the next session of this parliament.

speechtext: I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Now that the first quarter of the year has been completed in the government's program for support prices for eggs, can the minister inform the house whether deficiency payments are necessary to bring the national average of producer prices up to the level of the support price? speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
On January 111 announced that the agricultural stabilization board would make an interim payment to producers for eggs marketed during the period January 1 to March 31. I also pointed out that at that time egg marketings were at a relatively high level, and that this interim payment was being made to provide assistance to producers during the period of adjustment.

Inquiries of the Ministry
The national weighted average price lor grade A large eggs during the period January 1 to March 31 was 25.4 cents per dozen, or 7.6 cents below the prescribed national weighted average support price of 33 cents per dozen.
In establishing the exact amount of the deficiency payment, the agricultural stabilization board took into account the fact that the national weighted average price of grade A large eggs during the last quarter of 1959 was slightly below the prescribed price, and will accordingly pay an interim deficiency payment of 8 cents per dozen. This payment will be made for all grade A large and extra large eggs up to a total of 1,000 dozen, marketed in the period January 1 to March 31, 1960, by producers registered with the agricultural stabilization board. Cheques will be mailed to producers as soon as marketing records for this quarter are completed, which is expected to be within the next few days.
During the period January 1 to March 26, 1960, egg marketings were 7 per cent below marketings for the same period in 1959, and for the week ending March 26 marketings were 12 per cent below the same week a year ago.
The reduction in egg marketings is now reflected in improving price levels. Egg marketings are now in a more realistic balance with domestic requirements, and except for seasonal variations prices may be expected to remain at or above the support level. During the week of March 26 the national weighted average price for all grades of eggs in Canada was 34.9 cents per dozen, or 1.9 cents above the support price, as compared to the national weighted average price for the same week a year ago of 31.9 cents when the board was purchasing eggs to support the price.
The deficiency payments of 8 cents per dozen on grade A large eggs, which will be paid to all producers regardless of location, is
0.4 cents per dozen higher than producers in Alberta and Saskatchewan would have received under a regional average basis, and
0.4 cents less than the producers in Manitoba would have received.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, March 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming 79951-0-181*
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson (Eglinton) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be the first one to admit that the Minister of Finance is not easy to follow in debate. I was interested to read of a delegation that visited the Prime Minister during the middle of last month, inviting him to a summit meeting of the chiefs of the Six Nations Indian reserves, an invitation which was, by the way, declined. None the less the delegation afterwards reported:
We have had a lot of promises in the past that have never been kept.
But the spokesman said, after an hour with the Prime Minister:
He is a great talker. He can almost make you forget what you came here for.
I think that was about the position of those in the gallery the other night because, next to the Prime Minister, I would certainly give full marks to the Minister of Finance for being this house's greatest illusionist.
We have some sympathy for the Minister of Finance. Admittedly he has had difficult circumstances to contend with, but we would have more sympathy were it not for our feeling that many of the difficult circumstances have been of his own making. I said the other night-and I think a number of other commentators are confirming the view-that the presentation was really a do nothing budget. Someone amended that by saying, "Well, if it was not a do-nothing budget it was then perhaps doing just the same as was done last year." I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is not good enough.
One has to do quite a bit of searching through ore to try to find a bit of sparkle in this budget. I have been prepared to do that, and I have, of course, every desire to approve of some of the good new items, however slender, that appear there. I think most hon. members will approve of the minister's announcement that the double impact of income and estate taxes on pension and annuity rights inherited by widows and others will be avoided.
I remind the minister, of course, that when the new estate tax was being examined in the committee on banking and commerce, sitting when the house was sitting, I stood alone and indicated that the women's organizations of Canada, including the university women and the national council of women, even trust companies and others who were familiar with these matters, urged that this particular amendment be taken care of at that time. I was voted down, of course, by the

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson overwhelming majority of government supporters in that committee. I think too there will be universal approval of the minister's proposal to increase the exemption with respect to medical expenses, for the benefit of those who are faced with abnormally high expenses these days when such expenses admittedly are rising very noticeably.
It was the Winnipeg Free Press, as the minister might imagine, that made the statement last year that it is not realistic to expect an opposition to penetrate all the deceptions of an often deceptive government. I, of course, would not hope to be able to do that today. However, in reading the resolutions over the week end I did notice some items that have not had adequate attention perhaps to date by the taxpayers. I think, for instance, of resolution No. 7 with respect to the sales tax. This is the way that resolution reads:
That portrait photographs of individuals be exempt from sales tax.
I suppose the uninformed may have taken a little glow from the thought that in getting portraits next Christmas they may be able to benefit from what looks like a reduction in tax. Without any explanation, as is usual in these matters, it would appear that this is not a reduction in taxation. Portraits have been exempt from the sales tax. On the contrary, this vehicle is being used to impose new taxation that has not been imposed hitherto. I think this is a very regrettable, back door and sly method of introducing a new tax. I suppose the minister is following the slogan of the popular song; he is simply "emphasizing the positive". But what is actually happening here is that for the first time it seems it is the intention of the minister to impose a tax on developing the films used in our amateur photography, which you and I take to have developed in the ordinary photographer's shop. So I came to the realization that quite contrary-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite wrong.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the minister deny that portraits have always been exempt from tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will deny that there is any suggestion of putting a tax on films that are being developed for people, as the hon. member has indicated.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am glad, we shall watch for developments.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Darkroom tactics.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do know that the minister's colleague the Minister of National


Revenue advised photo developers that it was the intention to impose this tax for the first time, effective in January of this year, without any change by means of a budget resolution but simply relying on what the department thought was permissive power in the present law. They took the matter to the Department of Justice. It is my submission that we have here a clear exemption of one type of portrait photography with the intention of going ahead with the proposal to impose a sales tax for the first time on the ordinary development of films. If I am wrong I will be very pleased to hear so from the minister.
Before we proceed too far with the budget debate, and in view of the fact that in the city of Ottawa the civil service pension plan covers more people than any other such plan elsewhere, I suggest that the effects of income tax resolution No. 12 be considered by taxpayers very carefully. As most of us know, under certain circumstances a person can withdraw from the civil service pension plan and receive a lump sum payment. This provision is utilized particularly by single female employees upon marriage. The intent of the resolution may be simplification for the tax collector, but we must examine very carefully the effect upon the taxpayer himself.
Apart from some of these items, I do not see that it is useful at this stage, or until we come to debate the resolutions, to refer very much to some of the other items because not very many people are interested in cuttlefish, fish bait, pretzels, instant potatoes and the like, which are prominent in the resolutions this year. At another stage I do, of course, propose to examine very carefully the changes in the tariff. For three budgets we have seen the Minister of Finance come before us as he does, warming his coat tails before the glow of his professed virtue in tariff matters, but with each budget that has been presented we know we have had certain complaints from our best customers. I refer to Britain, Italy, Japan and so on. I suggest that again this year these items will require very careful consideration when we have the bill before us amending the Customs Tariff.
When I spoke briefly the other night, Mr. Speaker, there were a lot of oh's and ah's when I made the statement that the Minister of Finance had been 50 per cent wrong in his forecast of the gross national product, because he had made his forecast on the assumption that no increases in prices would be involved. Over the week end I think most of us have seen that this view has been shared by those

with prominent positions in financial journalism. I find that in the April 2 issue the Financial Post had this to say:
Business planners got an unwanted and unexpected surprise this week: 1959's gross national product made only a bare 3.5 per cent gain in volume. At budget time last year, finance minister Fleming had assumed that prices would be stable and a "real" 7 per cent advance would be achieved in the production of goods and services ...
These G.N.P. trends add to the evidence pointing to slower paced growth in 1960.
I hope the Minister of Finance will comment on this as we proceed. I hope the Financial Post is equally right when it goes on to say:
But it's probably all to the good, say most business analysts. The fewer the excesses this year, the milder any subsequent recession.
However, that was not the minister's forecast last year and, as I indicated, it was just 50 per cent out with respect to volume and an assumption of no increases in prices. When we examined the minister's comments the other night we were greatly disappointed with regard to some of the important matters other than finance lightly dealt with that have a great effect upon our economy and' our financial future. There was certainly cavalier treatment with respect to the problem of unemployment. It was certainly brushed under the rug. In the budget of the Minister of Finance we seemed to have quite a departure from the philosophy of the Prime Minister that "no man is going to suffer". There is nothing new for the unemployed. In fact one could hardly find anything more fatuous than this brief reference to unemployment in the minister's statement, as found at page 2670 of Hansard:
I am confident... that employment will rise as the coming of spring opens up new job opportunities and as the economy continues its upward trend.
What a shame.

If that is all that can be expected, if that is all the minister was prepared to tell us in his budget speech about the pressing problem of unemployment, I say it is cavalier treatment indeed. About agriculture there was nothing at all said. The silence was deafening with respect to our agricultural industry. Notwithstanding the fact that the net income of Canadian farmers as reported, last month, has declined 7 per cent in 1959, did the minister make any comment about that very vital industry in his report to the nation the other night? He did not.
Well, Mr. Speaker, at this stage in our proceedings it is always monotonous-it is monotonous to us as it must be to those on
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson the other side-and indeed depressing to recite even a partial list of the broken promises of this administration. I believe those promises were made not with the feeling that they would ever have to be redeemed, but were made in an election campaign simply from the point of view of embarrassment.
I shall refer to some very briefly. There was the promise to reduce expenditures, and then what happened? They were increased. There was the promise to lower taxes, but they were raised; the denunciation of high interest rates, and they were pushed higher; the promise to provincial governments of benefits which the government find afterwards they seemingly cannot concede; the promise to divert trade from the United States and then they concentrate trade more in the single basket; the promise to cure unemployment, and in the year which our financial treasurer says is a prosperous year we find unemployment worse than last year and rising. There was the promise to reorganize and rationalize national defence. Now, there is almost universal agreement across the country that national defence is in an incomprehensible mess.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that in this picture two things have come into focus. It has become abundantly clear that the Prime Minister is, after all, mortal; and second, that the taxpayers' purse is limited. The taxpayers had begun to wonder if the vision was something they could actually afford or was merely an illusion. What are some of the results? We find that the Minister of Finance today is the one being cheered, mostly, as the strong man of the day. The "no person will suffer" philosophy, as I have said, seems to have been jettisoned as being incompatible with the green light that, at some stage, apparently was given to the Minister of Finance to make our finances more sound. Even the government itself now appears to be reaping the whirlwind of the iniquitous promise seed which it sowed in two elections.
At some point last fall-I think this is very interesting-even the Prime Minister seems to have got green around the gills in connection with our financial distress and must have decided on something new because, after all, a change did take place. The Minister of Finance has given us a review of the past year, but it seems to me that the white paper and his report to the house last Thursday night have left out a great portion of the real bases for some of the changes that have taken place.
I want to ask the house to reflect upon the climate, financial and political, across this country last year, particularly in the

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson fall. I have a little review to show just what the thinking was of people not only in this country, of those likely to be biased in favour of the government, but of onlookers outside of the country. What were they saying six months ago? The Economist of London, an outstanding United Kingdom journal, described Canada as in a financial mess.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Will the hon.
gentleman read some of the articles from those English papers that came out about six weeks or two months later, and which corrected those erroneous statements?

That was doubtless after the visit by the minister of the United Kingdom, when he said that Canada's finances were as sound as a bell. But it was also after the time that radical changes were made in the direction of our finances in this country.
The Globe and Mail of Toronto has never been particularly unfriendly to this government. Its financial editor, after hearing the speech of the Prime Minister on our financial policy which was delivered to the Lethbridge chamber of commerce, said this:
As to the cause of tight money, this may clearly be attributed to official policy.
The Montreal Star commented as follows:
We wish that someone he would listen to. would tell the Prime Minister that no one cares whether tight money is due to the Liberals, the Conservatives or hurricane Gracie. Very tight money is here.
Tight money is due to a combination of factors for some of which the government has responsibility. Why not tell what government policy is? Mr. Diefenbaker could. Instead we have to go on guessing.
This was the climate of last fall. The money market certainly told the government that something was wrong and not sound as a bell. I think you and I as individuals, if we had found it so difficult to borrow money, certainly would have thought something was wrong with our operations and would be rather concerned. At the beginning of October the president of the investment dealers of Canada had this to say:
The underlying issue is the absence of leadership by the government in monetary matters.
The financial editor of the Montreal Gazette, commenting on that statement by the representative of the investment dealers, said this-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman give the date of the quotations?

October 1, 1959 was the date of the first one. Commenting on that statement the following day the financial

editor of the Montreal Gazette, not unfriendly to this government either, said if that statement of the I.D.B. is to be criticized, the criticism is that the statement has not gone far enough.
Within about a week, in this kind of climate -and I am giving only a few illustrations of what was being said about the financial policy of the government-it is true that the Minister of Finance broke a long silence, something which is unusual for him, and made a statement to the Empire club of Toronto. This followed within a few days that famous television broadcast of the Prime Minister when he delved into financial policy and pouted that the banks were to blame for our situation and said that nobody was going to stampede him.
Within a week we certainly did get from the Minister of Finance something quite different and more positive in connection with financial policy. It appeared that at long last the Minister of Finance had been given by his Prime Minister something in the way of a brighter light with respect to financial leadership in the country. We certainly had been in quite a bit of uncertainty previously. I should like to give an illustration of what the House of Commons was told in the previous session by the Minister of Finance as to financial policy, and the kind of muddled explanation that we obtained. As reported at page 3746 of Hansard of May 18, a question was put to the Minister of Finance and these were his words in reply:
If the banks find they have not an ample amount of money to meet the extraordinary demands for credit that are made upon them today as a result of the upsurge in the Canadian economy, then certainly it is not the intention of the Canadian government to inflict on the people of Canada a repetition of the tight money policy of our Liberal predecessors.
Then the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate asked this question: "What are you going to do to stop it?" To that question there was no answer. There was no answer after the adjournment of the house until the minister started in October to make statements as he has been doing, as I said the other night, every month since. What is the policy? Is the policy that the budget is to be balanced at any cost, or is it the policy enunciated previously by the Prime Minister, namely that no person will suffer-presumably economically-in this country?
The Minister of Finance the other night had quite a bit to say about debt management. There was a striking absence of comment on unemployment and agriculture. However, he had a great deal to say about debt management. I think some of the statements made

the other night are certainly worthy of a review. As reported at page 2677 of Hansard the minister said this:
-the total volume of direct government of Canada marketable issues outstanding at the end of the year is only $28 million higher than at the beginning.
What is the unsophisticated person going to think about that statement? I suggest to the Minister of Finance that no matter how he may twist or squirm, all he requires to do is look at the statistics in the weekly report of the Bank of Canada-and I refer to the latest one, dated March 31 of this year- and he will find that the total of government of Canada direct and guaranteed securities outstanding is up $756 million from a year ago. This is the sum that was taken by the government from the market, and taking this sum diminished accordingly the amounts which investors would otherwise have had available for other undertakings, for other governments, for the commerce of the country and so on. I say, Mr. Speaker, what lubricity there is in this kind of statement.
The finance minister's remarks on the debt management activities of the government in the past 12 months just glossed over the tremendous damage that his borrowings have caused to junior governments and to individual commercial borrowers. The course of the treasury bill rates during the year 1959 reflects these repeated demands made by the government on the money market. The Minister of Finance suggests that these rates really, in their rise, reflected particularly the heavy demands that were made by ordinary commerce through the banks. It was the earlier demands of this government for money, made through and after the conversion loan, that demoralized the interest rates of this country and made it no longer possible for the Minister of Finance to say, "look what we as a government have done to bring down interest rates". Once they started to rise, of course, it was somebody else's fault. First of all it was said it was that of the Bank of Canada; then it was said it was the fault of the chartered banks of the land. But the course of the rise is evident. It stemmed and originated from that unfortunate conversion loan.
Give the most recent Bank of Canada rate.

I am going to refer to that matter. I suggest that the hon. member, like the Minister of Finance, may claim credit that it is going down. You are taking great credit for it going down, but refused to accept any responsibility for financial policy when it was going up to heights never experienced in a generation. I want to say something about what this has resulted in. Let us look at what
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson the cost of interest has meant to this government-and we are examining the accounts of our government for the past year-quite irrespective of the calamity that its policies have caused in pushing out other governments and pushing out the legitimate commerce of the land.
The main estimates for 1960-61 provide for interest in a staggering sum, but this is not all the story. The amount of interest actually provided in the book of estimates for the forthcoming year is less than was spent by the government last year. The amount is $594 million. The actual interest charges last year amounted to $632 million. I pointed out the other night that there is an allowance of only $140 million for extra charges for the remainder of this new year if he is actually to produce a balanced budget. The other night he provided $15 million for the civil servants. But here is a difference of $39 million between what was actually spent last year on interest and what is provided for in the estimates for interest for the coming year.
The question that naturally arises is this. Can the minister, with an item of this kind and many others that I could mention, hold the line to this margin of $140 million in the large budget that is involved for this country? We know this government has indicated that as far as freight rates are concerned, an increase cannot be allowed. They have said that the line must be held. Indeed, the president of the Canadian National Railways said to our committee the other day that if freight rates went up he thought there would perhaps be a diminishing return to the railroads. In competition with other carriers the freight carried would become less. We have at the present time a board of conciliation with respect to the wage demands of 100,000 of our railway employees. If freight rates are to be held as they are and subsidies are to be continued in order to provide wage increases commensurate with increases in wages to workers in other segments of the economy, what is that going to do to the budget of the Minister of Finance?
The minister always has a desire to relate the national debt to per capita debt. We are sorry that we have not in the house these days the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan). We hope, however, that he will be back with us after an operation after the Easter recess, at which time he will doubtless be participating in later stages of this debate. But I am surprised the Minister of Finance would repeat this old tale after the excellent way in which it was presented to the house last year, when the hon. member for Welland pointed out that what the minister was really saying was that every baby

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson born and every immigrant arriving into the country is simply being handed and assuming a share of the debt. The member for Welland also pointed out that this does not in any way reduce the debt by one dollar. It is simply a matter of transferring to a new baby a share of the public debt.
The net debt as it stands today is $12.1 billion. The Liberals, so much attacked by the Minister of Finance in the past when he sat in opposition for reaching large surpluses, as a result reduced the net debt over a period of 11 years from $13.4 billion to just over $11 billion. In two years this new administration has managed to wipe out half the savings achieved by their predecessors over a period of 11 years.
The cost of servicing the public debt, as a result of the high interest rates and unprecedented deficits in peacetime, now stands at $786 million. This is the second largest item in our budget, being second only to that for national defence. Let us look at the cost of servicing this debt today per wage earner. If we take the figure for the total labour force as approximately 6,200,000, I calculate that the cost would be $126 per year or about $10.50 per month for each wage earner in this country to service the debt. This, of course, is a tremendous obligation, and it has been rising to great proportions.
Mr. Speaker, in connection with debt management, I want to look at another angle. In examining the Bank of Canada report I have found there set out the details of the various forms of loans obtained last year by this administration. We have features that have never been prominent in requests for money over many years of this country's history. Loan after loan seems to have coupled with it a new gimmick and I suggest something which one would almost regard as a new give-away, so far as the taxpayers are concerned, in order to get money.
I refer to such things as the non-callable feature. We have had non-callable features in our public debt in the past, it is true; but I pointed out in the budget debate last year, when referring to the conversion loan which was made, that it would be a financial tragedy of great magnitude when the youth of this land, when they became taxpayers, found there were no callable features as far as. the government was concerned respecting that massive conversion involving $6.4 billion.
This has continued. In the past there were occasionally times under the previous administration when the callable feature was omitted, but I suggest there is a very big difference between the elimination of a callable feature when interest rates are 3 per cent and 3J per cent and when they are 6J per cent or 5J per cent, at all time high levels.


This is what the Minister of Finance is denying to his successors in the way of financial adjustment in the future if interest rates go down.
I refer to the debate of last year of March 18, when I said there was another very dangerous gimmick which the minister was apparently introducing. That was the gimmick of a very substantial discount offered with respect to a very short term loan. I do not know whether the minister was as naive as he suggested, whether he actually did not realize the implication of this, or whether he was endeavouring to mislead me or put me and the hon. member for Welland off. Also the Leader of the Opposition-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must take objection to the imputation in the words used by the hon. gentleman. He has his opportunity to withdraw that expression, when he suggests I was misleading him.

I withdraw willingly, the words "misleading me," Mr. Speaker, and in doing so I will indicate that if one reads the remarks of the Minister of Finance as they appear in Hansard of March 18 of last year, it will be found that he said in reply to remarks made by the hon. member for Welland, "What difference does the length of the term make?" We had described the value to shrewd, sophisticated investors of getting a substantial discount on the purchase of a government bond and utilizing that, if they were not dealers, as a tax free capital gain. Indeed, one wonders why, if it were not deliberate tailoring, we had what would normally be called a treasury bill which would not be subject to a capital gain advantage, but by tailoring the loan for merely a period of one more month, 13 months, it was called a bond.
I pointed out last year that as a bond this was indeed a very expensive form of floating loans on the part of the Minister of Finance. He did not seem to realize that the discount portion of the loan extending over 12 of the 13 months was worth more to a person or a corporation paying income tax of 50 per cent than was the nominal rate advertised with respect to it across the country, the low and unrealistic

rate advertised at that time being 2f per cent. I said at that time that for a taxpayer who was paying an effective income tax rate of 50 per cent, and who was entitled to a capital gain, it was equivalent to a rate of 6.6 per cent for a bond sold at 100 cents for the dollar. I said in addition that I thought the Minister of Finance was suggesting in this form of procedure, providing short term bonds, a form of finance to the junior governments, and that as the collector of most of the income tax in this country he would regret it very keenly as time went on.
Some of the governments, following the example of course of the Minister of Finance, have been entering into this type of financing to a much bigger extent than ever before, and the sufferer is the treasury of Canada which does not get, on the difference between par and the discounted price, any income tax if the purchaser of the bonds is not a dealer and is thus entitled to have the discount regarded as a capital gain. I think this reached proportions of a dangerous nature. The Minister of Finance did not take that advice, and during the year we had subsequent floatings of loans with this important discount feature over a short term. I say this is going to prove very expensive indeed to the other side of the government, the tax collecting department, when they are seeking to collect income tax.
Then toward the fall we got into something which I think is particularly frightening to the young people of the land, if they just care to look at the type of financing which the minister has embarked upon. I have already said that most of his loan flotations do not give him the right, if interest rates go down substantially in the future, to call the debt, as used to be the practice when interest rates were nothing like as high as these. But here, time after time from September on we have had loan issues which have no call right and another feature called the right to convert. In other words, the sophisticated borrower sees that he has all the benefits of the present high rates of interest for bonds maturing over a short period of time, in 1962, 1963 and 1964, and then if rates of interest prevailing in this country in those years are substantially less he has the right to extend the term of those loans, in some cases up to an additional 13 years.
One can readily recognize this form of finance is certainly going to prove very costly indeed to the taxpayers of tomorrow, who are the youth of today; and this in spite of the fact we have indicated these dangers to the Minister of Finance in the past.
Then we come to Canada savings bonds. Even the Auditor General suggested that 79951-0-182
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson there seemed to be a lot of unnecessary and expensive run-around with respect to this form of finance. Canada savings bonds, when they were introduced by the previous administration, may have had some social benefit. They were tailored to encourage savings on the part of the small individual of the land. The maximum amount under the previous administration available to any individual was set at $5,000. Under the new administration there has developed another sales gimmick. The bonds formerly never available to other than the small man, are now available to estates and trusts. They are available to an amount of $20,000 in the name of any one individual, instead of being available to a total of $5,000. I do not think this can be called a small man's form of lending his savings to the government.
The minister's report shows that in the fiscal year just past he did, it is true, sell $1,455 million worth of Canada savings bonds at extraordinary high rates of interest. But the report also shows, at page 267 of Hansard -and this is also contained in the white paper-that the minister in the same year redeemed $1,170 million of Canada savings bonds. In other words he has just been rolling this debt over, and the net increase in borrowings of this nature was only $285 million during the year as shown by this report.
This has even provoked complaints from provincial treasurers. When it had some social merit, providing a vehicle for lending money in small amounts, as under the previous administration, up to a limit of $5,000, these complaints did not arise; but the minister will have noticed that the treasurer of his own province of Ontario has long since cried "ouch" and "foul" against this practice, and only last week these were the words used in the legislature by the premier of Ontario with respect to this type of federal financing:
I do not agree with what they are doing. I feel it is totally unfair. It is "hot'' money, and the turnover is tremendous.
I have indicated that the minister cannot have this both ways. I suggest to him that he is always criticizing the opposition and saying we are the prophets of doom and gloom. I say to him that the biggest prophet of doom today is the Minister of Finance if he thinks we shall have this tight money situation with us so long that in 1962, 1963 and 1964 he must be prepared to give lenders an option to renew their loans at 1959 and 1960 rates of interest for high interest rates such as are indicated in the Bank of Canada report; for another 13 years, seven years and
