The Budget-Mr. Benidickson so on. I say he is the pessimist if he thinks that interest rates at levels such as we are experiencing at the present time are to continue for 13 years or more.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made some comment on the fact that in the last month the rate being paid for treasury bills has fallen very substantially. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that this being so he might get in touch with the commercial arm of the Bank of Canada and see if something could not be done to reduce the rate of interest being charged by the industrial development bank to commercial oorrowers.
This would have a very healthy effect upon business in this country, and would provide a healthy stimulus. In March 1959 this government bank raised its charge to borrowers from 6 per cent to 6J per cent. Last October 1 it increased the rate again from 6| per cent to 7 per cent. I suggest that in view of this drop in the treasury bill rate from about 6 per cent last September to 3.26 per cent on March 30 last, the minister might consider carefully whether business would not be stimulated if borrowers who cannot go into the securities market or whose applications are turned down by the chartered banks were able to obtain a decent rate of interest from the government bank itself.
Now with respect to revenue and taxes, 1 have indicated what were some of the promises made by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister when they sought a mandate from the people of this country. What do the white paper and the speech of the minister the other night indicate? The minister, of course, compared taxes with the gross national product. Well, we all take pride in the growth of Canada, but most of us think that if a man is progressing in his business and taking in more money he should be expected to get out of debt rather than be complacent about staying in debt.
Apart from that, let us look at the following table. I think, as I have said, that the gross national debt is not being reduced but only being spread more widely; that it is being shared by a greater number of newborn babies. I submit that a more realistic table with respect to tax revenues would certainly have reference to the amount of taxes per capita which are being paid.
I should like to submit a table which I have prepared. It shows a comparative statement of revenues. The figures in each case are taken from the budget papers, and the table compares the revenues taken by this administration in respect of ordinary budgetary expenditures and the old age security fund in 1958-59 with the estimate given the


other night for 1960-61. This indicates that the tax revenues per capita in 1958-59 are $269.48 and in 1960-61, $326.72. That is a very substantial increase indeed, and this from an administration led by a gentleman who went up and down Canada saying taxation would be reduced.
I have here a headline taken from the Toronto Globe and Mail shortly after the present Prime Minister was elected to the leadership of his party. It reads, "Diefenbaker charges Liberals are Pickpockets". Now, when the tax take is considered, comparing revenues two years ago with the expectations for the coming year, I wonder what the people of this country will think of that kind of political propaganda. This was a speech made on a program of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation during a free-time period.
Indeed, it was in the same speech that the Prime Minister indicated that the Conservative party would have a commission set up to report on government economies which might be put into effect. It is almost three years since hon. gentlemen opposite took charge of the government, and this commission has yet to be established. We know that any inquiry as extensive as the one proposed would take several years to complete, and I say this is just a further indication of somersaulting with regard to promises made to the Canadian people in 1957 and 1958 elections.
When we come to consider expenditures we find something which is just as revealing. If we look at the budget papers we find the expenditure reported there for the last full year of the Liberal administration, 1956-57. The total, including old age security payments, amounted to $5,228 million. In the year just ended-and I am not taking the figures for the year ahead; that would show an even bigger disparity-in the year which was reported upon the other night by the Minister of Finance, we find that there is a billion dollar difference since this administration has been in office.
One thing which the Minister of Finance reported in his budget this year-and he did it in his budget speech last year-is the well worn claim, as it appears in Hansard on page 2679, to the effect that because of the very careful and exacting scrutiny of departmental estimates it is likely that there will not be the usual amount of government lapses, unspent moneys that are put into the budget.
The minister said exactly the same thing last year, as recorded at page 2413 of Hansard. These are, of course, good illustrations of the minister's usual modesty.

But bearing these remarks in mind and bearing in mind his suggestion that extraordinary scrutiny has been provided while he has been in charge of the Department of Finance, something presumably never equalled by his predecessors, let us examine the public accounts for 1958-59. We find there that the main estimates for 1958-59 indicated statutory expenditures of $1,788 million. But the accounts show that total budgetary expenditures under statutory authorization amounted to $1,970 million. In other words, the reality was worse than the prospect.
But these are statutory items. What unusual, extraordinary control has been proposed with respect to the items the minister sometimes describes as controllable? In other words, they are voted by parliament. In the main and various supplementary estimates submitted to parliament by the minister authority was given to him to spend $3,818 million in 1958-59. The actual expenditures for those same items amounted to only a difference of $424 million. Does anybody think that careful control, as indicated by the minister, was applied if we have lapsings of $424 million and if as he says, under his supervision presiding over treasury board these estimates of expenditures had received care and attention beyond that of any other of his well-known predecessors. I am afraid the minister is going to sprain his shoulder one of these days patting himself on the back. The trouble is, when one examines these lapsings one finds that it is so unnecessary.
At this stage it is very difficult for anybody examining the budget papers which were presented to us the other day to make a complete and accurate calculation to see how well the minister has carried out his boast in the next year 1959-60 with respect to the close control of the estimates so that lapsings would be minimal. However, by the use of the budget papers it is possible to make a calculation in this respect. Out of budgetary expenditures under statutory appropriations of $2,253 million I do admit that it is not readily possible to follow $21.3 million of expenditures, but with respect to the remainder of this large sum of $2,253 million it is possible to relate the expenditures reported in the 1960 white paper back to the book of estimates for 1959-60 which was prepared by the minister. When one does that he finds that it was proposed in the blue book that $2,056 million be spent on statutory items as appropriations for 1959-60. As I say, in both cases, I have deleted miscellaneous items of approximately $21 million. When this is examined we will find-and I think this is of interest when we consider the 79951-0-1824
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson narrow margin upon which the minister is basing his surplus for next year-that there was an increase of $196 million. I have indicated on how narrow a base the margin is for the minister's next year's surplus.
With respect to non-statutory authorizations voted in supply I find that there were lapsings of $288.6 million. When one examines the records of previous years, he finds this does not indicate to him that the minister has been better able to reduce lapsings under non-statutory appropriations and at times overexpenditures under statutory items than his predecessors.
It was rather amusing the other night to find that this was brought forward again by the minister despite this discrepancy, when one looks to the past two years' record. It is reported that the other night the Minister of Finance went up to the press gallery after delivering his budget address. One of the journalists asked him a question. It is reported in this way:
He fenced nimbly with a reporter who asked him if the modest $12 million surplus was over-taxation, a sin for which the one-time opposition critic used to castigate the Liberal government.
"That was different," said Mr. Fleming. ''The Liberals were guilty of inaccurate budgeting."
I have indicated the kind of lapsings and discrepancies between the estimates of the Minister of Finance in each of two years.
I indicated some kinds of promises that remain unfulfilled. In fact, what we are getting now demonstrates leadership diametrically opposite to what was indicated to the electorate would be their policy in the matter of finance.
However, the Minister of Finance last year spoke for the second time in the budget debate, as reported at page 2892 of Hansard of April 21, 1959. This shows the extreme length to which the minister can go in debate in the house. He was dealing with the opposition amendment at that time a year ago, and he said:
I have dealt with the terms of this extraordinary amendment, an amendment which has the temerity to accuse this government of having made promises which it did not make; of having been elected on the basis of promises which it did not give during the election campaign, and of having broken promises which it did not make.
I leave it to the country to decide whether any of the promises I have referred to today are not promises that were made well known across Canada as promises made by hon. members of the administration who now sit on the treasury benches. If that is not enough, let us look at some other promises, promises that related to likely changes in fiscal policy.
There are, of course we have been told, two kinds of promises. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) has indicated

The Budget-Mr. Benidickson that promises made outside the house are not entitled to the same respect and obligation as promises made in the house, and I must confess that some of these promises were made outside the house but by very prominent members of the Conservative party.
Just promises to the people.

Just promises to the
people. We remember that at the national convention at which the present Prime Minister was elected leader of his party they had a resolutions committee. It is true that they did draw up a number of items for the platform for the election that was expected to take place in six months or so afterwards. But after the election of the present Prime Minister as party leader it seems that these platform items were stifled. However, those of use who were here at that time know that no one had a better entree to the goings-on at that convention and to the activities of the Conservative party than that good friend of all of us, Mr. Blakely, representing the Montreal Gazette.
Before these plans in the platform were thrown out we had a report from Mr. Blakely as to the goings-on in the resolutions committee of the Conservative party. In the Montreal Gazette of December 12, 1956 he reported that the party had agreed, through its resolutions committee, on an extension of the housing act to cover existing homes in good condition. We have heard no more about that. It was agreed that they would encourage processing in Canada. What is there in this budget along these lines of fiscal policy. It was indicated that they would encourage national research by a more favourable tax climate. I see the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy): I have no doubt he is still trying to persuade the government to carry out this part of the platform. He probably had a great deal to with getting it in there in the first place. We find that they proposed the development of a deep sea fleet at an estimated cost for 35 ships of some $35 million. That has gone down the drain. Even what we had under the previous administration was sold by this administration.
Sold to Batista.

They promised that they would eliminate the sales tax on purchases by school boards. This is the third budget presented by the minister and we have had nothing with respect to that yet. Then there is another matter which is of great concern to me because I have a bill on the order paper to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act with the same objective that the Conservative party had in 1956, that of providing aid to non-industrial small business through the industrial development bank.

When that bill comes up for consideration I hope that my friends, who in such large numbers form the governing party, will make sure of the passage of the bill.
Here is an amazing one. They proposed that they would withdraw from the taxation field with respect to alcoholic beverages and would leave that field entirely to the provinces. Some credit was given to individual sponsors of resolutions at that convention. The present member for Calgary South (Mr. Smith)-he was not a member then-said that he won his case before the 162 member policy and resolutions committee when he called for an amendment to provide for tax concessions for Canadian oil and gas operators equal to those obtained by United States operators from the United States government. We just heard the other day that the government, after almost three years of responsibility, were finally removing the road block that they themselves created instead of providing a green light for this very important industry in western Canada.
Here is another interesting one. The former member for Gloucester got his way too when he insisted that the word "distinctive" be used to describe the Canadian national flag to be adopted immediately.
We know that these planks in the platform were pigeonholed, but let us look at the matter from another angle.
What about the excise tax on automobiles?

The excise tax on automobiles was another example. In the election campaign the Conservative party made no reference to the promises made at the national convention and in substitution therefor said that they would go by the commitments made to the Canadian people by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), then the party leader. It just happens that many matters having direct reference to fiscal policy were indeed referred to publicly and often by the Prime Minister. In his speech to the Montreal chamber of commerce shortly after his election as leader of the party he said that there would be tax changes if his party was elected to power to put Canadian companies on a basis of equality with foreign corporations or their subsidiaries operating in Canada. After three budgets what have we in the minister's financial proposals with respect to that matter?
Again, in his opening campaign speech in Toroto on April 25, 1957 the present Prime Minister said that there would be less discriminatory methods of taxing Canadian oil companies. This was the plank that the hon. member for Calgary South was instrumental

in selling to the 162-member convention resolutions committee. Again, as reported in the Vancouver Sun of March 10, 1958, the Prime Minister said that there would be drastic changes in the taxation treatment of all companies. He said that under the Income Tax Act further incentives would be provided for Canadians to invest in Canadian equity stocks. That was also in his opening campaign speech at Massey hall, Toronto, on April 25, 1957.
Then we come back to the project of the hon. member for Lambton West. Tax reductions to encourage Canadian research in every field, which was also referred to by the Prime Minister at Massey hall on the same date. At a Conservative rally at Campbell-ton, New Brunswick, on May 4, 1957 the Prime Minister promised tax inducements to persuade business firms to process raw materials in Canada.
As I say, these were promises made to the people of Canada outside the house and I think that most of us are disappointed to find little implementation of these well-known commitments made throughout the country in three budgets presented by the Minister of Finance.
I am not going to deal with this matter at any length. Not only in these monthly speeches of the Minister of Finance to chambers of commerce, empire clubs and others prior to presenting the budget but also in what he said to the House of Commons the other night, in which there was very little change from what he had been saying elsewhere, the minister closed his remarks by urging people, with that ring in his voice, to work and save. Of course, the poor unemployed would like to be able to work so that they could save. In past budget debates time after time the minister has used the Biblical reference about the mote and the beam and the eye. If the minister is trying to tell workers and people generally throughout the country that they should follow a policy of self-reliance and that there should be some forbearance and self-denial, I suggest that the minister simply look at the government telephone book of April, 1957 and the new directory and compare the number of staff for each of the ministers then with the number of personal, political staff now. I think the government is certainly not leading the way in forbearance, self-denial or, indeed, self-reliance.
A 50 per cent increase.

In department after department we find no indication of ministers seeking assistance from the permanent professional staffs of the department but rather
The Budget-Mr. Benidickson the addition of publicists, associate private secretaries, executive assistants, and so on. As somebody has said, the number is almost double what it was in 1957.
So I say that if the administration really desires to follow a policy of economy the ministry would be better advised, if they are not practicing self-reliance, to look to the permanent civil service for advice and counsel and not to political advisers to the extent that a comparison of the two telephone books indicates has taken place, contrary to their professions about economy. I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud):
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the financial policies of the government will produce a fourth consecutive over-all deficit in a year of "so-called prosperity", while at the same time offering no solution to the problem of rising prices, rising trade deficits, a continued high premium on the Canadian dollar, increased pressure on provinces and municipalities to borrow outside Canada, declining farm income, and high and rising unemployment."

I had hoped that the minister would have undertaken some moves to plug the many loopholes existing in our income tax laws at the present time. I had hoped there would, be a review of the extremely generous depletion and depreciation allowances that exist. We all hoped there would be an increase. allowed in the exemptions for the average wage earner in Canada and that the exemption for single people would have been raised at least to $1,500 and for married people to at least $3,000, with a much greater allowance for dependants than exists at the present time.
I had hoped that the government would have given some consideration to the institution of a graduated corporation tax in Canada. I cannot see the logic of applying a graduated income tax to individuals in Canada and yet having a flat percentage rate of corporation income tax. I feel that a graduated corporation tax would serve many useful purposes. It would make it a little bit easier for the small businessman to survive as a small independent businessman. It would be a weapon that would help to discourage the development of monopolies and cartels. It would reduce foreign investments to more reasonable levels. It would encourage the sale of offerings of federal, provincial and municipal governments on the money markets.
We had hoped that the government would at long last have instituted a capital gains tax which would also bring in its wake many helpful solutions to the problems of the Canadian economy. We talked about the difficulties-the premium on the Canadian dollar and investment by people in the United States in Canadian industrial enterprise-and the institution of a capital gains tax would be another method whereby in an orderly and planned manner we could bring about desirable results to the benefit of the future welfare of Canadians.
The minister hardly mentioned the field of agriculture. I suppose in the opinion of the Conservatives agriculture is no longer very important; at least, their action henceforth have not shown that they pay much attention to the needs of agriculture. I would like to ask what has happened to the demand for parity prices, and what has happened to the demand for deficiency payments when goods

are exported? There is no planning in this budget to grant either parity prices on home consumed good's or deficiency payments on exported goods.
Neither is there anything contained in the budget which will bring any measure of hope to what the minister admits is an average figure of 350,000 unemployed persons. May I point out to the minister and the government, in seeking ways and means of adding to its revenues, that if we had 350,000 as an average level of unemployment we thereby lost over $1 billion worth of wealth which would have gone into the Canadian economy. The attitude of the government of the day toward the unemployed of Canada seems callous indeed.
This Conservative government has now introduced the means test in the application of the Unemployment Insurance Act, a most regrettable move. The Unemployment Insurance Act was passed on insurance principles, and the introduction of the means test and the denying to these people of the benefits of their severance and holiday pay is completely opposed to the original intent of the act.
The independent businessman of Canada will receive small comfort from the budget. Ever since the Conservatives took office we have only had one lousy, measly $30,000 vote in all the estimates specifically designed to help the small businessman. How they were going to help the small businessman of Canada before the government was elected. Interest rates are now so high that they are beyond the ability of Canadian enterprise to afford. They are also beyond the reach of those responsible for supplying us with our social needs. Our municipalities, hospital boards and school boards simply are not doing the necessary borrowing because they feel that our home owners, in turn, can no longer pay these high interest rates on such borrowings. Our businessmen, especially our independent businessmen, have ended their major borrowings for the very same reason. They can no longer operate when they have to pay these excessive rates.
The government is deliberately responsible for raising the interest rate, and when one looks back now to the speeches made both by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and by the Prime Minister at the time of the bond conversion deal, he will realize that practically every one of the predictions and forecasts as to the blessings of this deal has since been denied by the facts.
We were assured that this move had to be made in order to rid the market of an excessive supply of short term securities. Yet after the bond conversion deal was completed the government itself simply flooded
The Budget-Mr. Regier the market with its short term securities, and the provinces and municipalities were not helped to market their own securities. There were many other forecasts and predictions made as to the wonderful blessings of this move, and I cannot think of a single prediction made by the minister at that time which he would now be willing to repeat in this house.
The government is responsible for making tight money tighter still. Tight money became tighter because of the desperate moves of the minister in the money market, and the banks of Canada had to bail out the government in order to make the bond conversion deal a success. The weekly statistics released by the Bank of Canada show that the minister's bond conversion deal would have been a flop if the banks had not come to his aid on an emergency basis. Of course, that made tight money tighter still, and the ordinary man just was not able to borrow.
Then the bottom fell out of the bond market, and in the words of one of the heads of the Canadian banks, the banks had to put a sounder foundation under the bond market and around about August of last year again had to come to the aid of the government and increase their holdings of bonds. Because of the interest rates being pushed up, large corporations left the market and went to the chartered banks in order to meet their capital needs. As a result, the small man in Canada has certainly had to take a beating.
The budget indicates no action will be taken to reduce the premium on the Canadian dollar which harms Canadian exporters so much and also works such a hardship on Canadian manufacturers. No action is indicated to increase our exports so that they may be more even with our imports. There is no action taken on behalf of the veterans of Canada so that their relative purchasing power in relation to the average wage earner of Canada can be restored to what it was shortly after the first world war. There is nothing in the budget to give any hope to those of us who look forward to more federal aid for education. Our municipalities certainly have nothing at all to their benefit from this budget.
We see nothing in it which will enhance economic aid or reduce defence spending. We see nothing in the budget which will encourage greater Canadian ownership of Canadian resources. There is nothing in the budget to deal with the serious transportation mess we are getting ourselves into and which will take hundreds of millions of dollars of public money to get us out of so as adequately to serve the needs of the nation. There is nothing in the budget to indicate

The Budget-Mr. Regier any awareness of the serious economic difficulties in the Atlantic areas of Canada. There is nothing in the budget for the masses of the Canadian people.
Our many problems were realized by the Conservative party and the Canadian people at the time of the last election. After three years what do we get? We get a speech from the throne that ignores these matters, and we get a budget which again refuses to recognize our difficulties. The budget contained a little bit for some civil servants. It was a balanced budget and a glowing report. Resolving our problems will take a lot of money. However, the wrong steps have already been taken by this government-inflation and getting more deeply into debt. The Tories have done both these things. The new budget of the Tories is a negative one. The only efforts they have undertaken have resulted in higher taxes, higher tariffs and higher interest rates.
The budget should be balanced by raising the productivity of the Canadian economic scene. We need vastly expanded production and all our people at work. We need more intensified production. Our whole economy is becoming more and more vulnerable to what happens in the United States of America. The glowing reports, when analysed, reveal that our prosperity is very narrowly based indeed and that an ever smaller number of Canadians are being allowed to share in the growing production and prosperity that we are said to have.
Moneylenders and foreign investors are having a field day in Canada. The government is applying the brakes to the development of the Canadian economy, and it is applying the brakes to a rising standard of living for most Canadian people. I appeal to the government to recognize that in this day and age its first responsibility is to the broad mass of the Canadian people. The people expect that their difficulties will be recognized and that action will replace pious appeals, and because we feel that the government, in the budget, is not recognizing its responsibilities to the Canadian people, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West:

speakeroldname: Mr. Richard A. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in what terms might I most appropriately describe the sallies and the sneers which have been launched against the budget this afternoon by opposition spokesmen? Having heard them, I thought that perhaps I should follow the example of the late Humphrey Mitchell, and speak in a kindly way. Is not what we have witnessed this afternoon a parade of the picayune, the piecemeal, the puerile and the perverse?
Have there been any objective, discriminating critiques of the budget, of fiscal or tax policy, or have we heard political harangues and abusive declamations? Have we heard constructive criticism, or churlish captiousness? The house and the country have a right to expect from the opposition's financial critics constructive, realistic, forthright and substantial criticisms. What they have received was a peddling of gloom, of pessimism, of despondency, of dejection. These qualities, however they may be a reflection of the political futures of the parties to which hon. gentlemen opposite belong, do not capture the mood of the Canadian people today and do not represent the reality of Canada's future, of her unprecedented and unparalleled development.
In what he had to say this afternoon about existing fiscal and taxation policies, did the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) propose any alternatives whatever? Did he give the house and the country any concept of the policies he would pursue in the unlikely and unhappy event of his becoming minister of finance? Carefully I listened to him, hoping for some clue. None did I gain, and none was there. With respect, may I say that his speech was in my opinion the most negative I have ever heard from a financial critic.
I am not one who believes that an opposition is under a duty to parade detailed policies on every issue. But I do affirm it has an obligation to assert its principles, to demonstrate on important fiscal matters where its principles and theories differ from those of the government. A hodge-podge of strictures is no alternative to statements of principle.
Presumably, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and others of the front bench of the group opposite-I adopt the word "group" to which they have been demoted by the hon. gentleman who represents Essex East (Mr. Martin)-will be speaking in this debate. Specifically and directly I invite them to state their fiscal principles, their economic tenets. Let them tell us what in this year 1960 would be their tax policy. Do

they believe in a balanced budget at this phase of our economy? What would they do about our deficit on international payments, except to talk about it? Would they stop the inflow of capital abruptly or gradually, completely or partially? Would they join their great expert Walter Gordon, who may become the minister of finance instead of the hon. gentleman from Kenora-Rainy River, and devalue the dollar, whatever that expression means? If it means something which technically it does not-merely reducing the value-how is that to be accomplished? Would foreign exchange control be reinstated? Would hon. gentlemen opposite peg a fixed rate of exchange and, if so, by what technique? Or would they go into the market and engage in a gigantic financial speculation in the purchase of foreign currencies? Have they, in fact, any cure which is not worse than the disease?
These are fair questions which I put to hon. members in the Liberal group. If we are to have an eight-day debate let it be a debate. Let us know where each party stands; let us get to grips with reality; let us thresh out the issues and the principles which are before us.
This amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River gives us no clues concerning Liberal policies. All it does is condemn; it does not assert. It is a warmed over version of the various amendments already proposed by the Liberal party to the address and on supply motions. I say to the hon. gentleman that the repetition of inaccurate assumptions-and that is all this amendment achieves-does not make them any more accurate or more palatable. I think I should add at once that the sophistical and unrealistic subamendment assuredly does not improve the amendment. In fact, I was thinking as I read through the text that both the amendment and the subamendment had obviously been drafted by experts, and I use the term "expert" in the sense in which Nicholas Murray Butler defined it, as one who knows more and more about less and less.
I do not propose at this time to spend any time replying to the speech of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier). That speech reminded me simply of one which Disraeli characterized as "the harebrained chatter of irresponsible frivolity". The hon. gentleman succeeded only in demonstrating one thing, the validity of the epigram of Viscount Hailsham: "The Left can never be Right". If the hon. gentleman is the spokesman of the so-called new and unnamed party of the left, its future might well be that described by a United States
The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell congressman who, speaking of another party, said it was "like a mule, without pride of ancestry or hope of posterity".
How old is that one? Why not say what you think instead of quoting the views of other people?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

May I say to the hon.
member that nothing becomes him so much as silence, and I hope he will observe it for a little while.
Let me deal with some of the matters which have been raised by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. In his anxiety to score debating points he fell into many grave errors this afternoon. Last Thursday night, and indeed again this afternoon he alleged that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had forecast for the last fiscal year an increase in the gross national product of 7 per cent, and in an imaginary horror he exclaimed that it was only 6 per cent. Let us test the validity of all his strictures by this one. What he forgot to tell the house was that the dominion bureau of statistics, after the last budget, revised upward the 1958 preliminary figure of gross national product, thereby involving a shift in the percentage by which 1959 could exceed it. What the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech of April 9, 1959-and I quote from Hansard at page 2409-was this:
I shall be basing my budgetary policy and my revenue forecasts on a gross national product of about $34) billion which is about 7 per cent above the average level achieved in 1958.
In other words the forecast was a dollar amount of $34J billion. What is the actual figure for 1959? It is $34,593 million, or $93 million more than the forecast figure. I ask this. Has the house ever seen closer estimating in respect of figures so astronomical? The margin of error is fantastically small.
Why, then, this talk of 6 per cent as opposed to 7 per cent? When the Minister of Finance brought down his budget on April 9, 1959 the preliminary estimate of the 1958 gross national product was $32,184 million. On this figure the forecast 1959 gross national product of $34J billion represented an increase of approximately 7 per cent. Later in 1959, the dominion bureau of statistics, on the basis of later information, adjusted the 1958 figure upwards from $32,184 million to $32,606 million, on which of course the percentage relationship was slightly less.
What my hon. friend failed to do was to compare the comparable. If you compare the

The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell preliminary 1958 figure of $32,184 million with the preliminary 1959 figure of $34,593 million you will find a 7.48 per cent increase.
This increase compares with the post-war average increase of about 4 per cent. In other words, our rate of growth in 1959 was almost double the average of other years since 1945, and this despite the fact that our rate of expansion was subject to a temporary but very significant pause in the third quarter of 1959, due to the effects of some major labour disputes. These are the real facts. But, in one of his scattered jibes on this subject, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River claimed that the Minister of Finance was 50 per cent wrong and he repeated that this afternoon.
In volume.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
My hon. friend was not 50 per cent wrong. He was 100 per cent wrong in this as in so many other subjects that he discussed.
For his forecast of the gross national product, his forecast of the budget deficit and other estimates, when compared with the actual, the Minister of Finance certainly need offer no apology. On the contrary, I believe he can proudly assert the smallest margins of error that there have been in history. Let hon. gentlemen opposite produce examples of any budget of recent Liberal ministers of finance where the forecast was so closely vindicated by actual performance, where the margin of error was less. All of us remember when time after time that very distinguished minister of finance, now Mr. Justice Abbott, would be $300 million and $400 million out in his forecast of budgetary balances. That was budgeting in those days by accident.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River attempted to find something sinister in the technique of dealing with the old age security fund. The Minister of Finance has loaned that fund $24 million, which amount will be repaid out of an anticipated $30 million surplus this year. Oh, said my hon. and genial friend from Kenora-Rainy River, if you had not done this your deficit would be $24 million greater. He cannot have it both ways although he tried to do just that very often this afternoon; he tried to have things both ways many times. Suppose he was right in the assertion which he makes; then, the inevitable concomitant would be that next year's surplus would be $30 million larger than that which has been forecast.
On many occasions this afternoon my hon. friend seemed to take great pleasure in playing with bookkeeping items. With great respect I would suggest to him that this hairsplitting brand of dialectics profits us not at all, and that he really should leave these


tactics to his colleague on the front bench who is an expert therein, namely the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith).
We heard some things this afternoon about unemployment. Not for a moment do I discount the individual problems which are involved. I could not do so, since it perhaps falls to my unfortunate lot to interview more persons seeking employment than perhaps any other hon. member of this house. But in their preachments of gloom, in their wal-lowings in pessimism these Jeremiahs opposite fail to tell us the whole story. It can be found in the white paper. There are more persons employed at better wages than at any time in our history. Total employment rose by
156,000	persons between 1958 and 1959. Labour income reached a record level of $17.7 billion, almost 8 per cent above 1958.. Since consumer prices roses only about 1 per cent, there was a substantial gain in real income.
A few weeks ago the Leader of the Opposition made a very realistic and I thought a surprisingly objective appraisal of some of the causes of unemployment and I think his example might be followed by some of his colleagues on the front bench opposite, particularly the hon. member for Essex East.
In all his declamatory rhetoric this afternoon, in his jibes the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River totally ignored the very substantial fiscal accomplishments of this government, the very genuine advances in fiscal and tax policy. I want to take a few moments to discuss ten of those highlights, adding the caution that this review and listing are not, of course, intended to be exhaustive or exclusive.
First, and at the top of my list, I put the successful financing of the greatest increases in social justice payments ever made in any period. What are the facts? Direct payments to individual Canadians by the federal government for social justice account have increased more than 50 per cent over the last year of Liberal government and that tremendous dollar increase has had to be financed from revenue.
This is all nonsense.

Will you allow me to deal with that now?

speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that is so. If he would only allow his statistical genius to have full sway he would discover the exact figures.
Would my hon. friend permit me to point out that whatever benefits there are-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My time is limited. My hon. friend's skill in building up men of straw is exceeded only by his volubility and ability to create diversionary tactics. I do not intend to be diverted in this way.
In the last year of Liberal administration old age security payments were $379 million; last year they were $574 million, an increase of about 52 per cent, and this is the story generally across the board.
Second, the fiscal policy of the government provided the incentive for recovery from the recession. In June of 1957 Canada was tottering on the verge of a depression. Had we not reversed some of the policies of our predecessors, recession would have become all-out depression. The reductions in taxes in 1957 and 1958, together with the introduction of many hundreds of million of dollars into housing, transportation and resources development, were designed to augment investment, to stimulate recovery and to provide employment. These policies succeeded.
Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to have forgotten that housing in Canada was coming to a virtual standstill when this government took office. It was the tremendous stimulus given the industry under the imaginative direction of the then minister of public works, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), that saved the day. The flexible and adjustable fiscal policies adopted by this government enabled the country to emerge from recession into recovery and renewed growth, and in the last fiscal period to experience an expansion of major magnitude as well as soundness.
Third, and in due course, has been the achievement of a balanced budget in the forthcoming fiscal year. For sound reasons the Minister of Finance deliberately budgeted for a substantial deficit in 1958 and for a reduced deficit in 1959. Two years ago we were meeting the problems, as I have said, of a recession and were seeking to use fiscal measures to offset the decline in business activity and to stimulate recovery. In 1960 our position is different. Deliberately, in this period of expansion, the government has brought the budget into a surplus position, a position where the federal government ceases to be a net borrower, thus leaving the capital market free to the extent of some $700 million to the provinces and the municipalities and to business and industry. Let
The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell no one think that this has been easily attained. Without the determination, the persistence and the tenacity of the Minister of Finance it could not have been accomplished. This balanced 1960 budget is a personal tribute to the hon. member for Eglinton.
The fourth major accomplishment of the government has been the achievement of relative price stability. No one can ever assert in a dynamic society the conquest of inflation. But we have accomplished an avoidance of disturbing fluctuations upwards or downwards in the general level of prices. In the last fiscal year of Liberal government the consumer price index rose 4.1 per cent. The first broken year of Liberal and Conservative government shows an increase of slightly less. Since that time, in two years the price index has risen 2.9 per cent or an average increase of less than 1.5 per cent a year. I say that ceaseless, unremitting vigilance to control inflationary pressures is essential to our progress, as the Minister of Finance so eloquently mentioned in his budget speech the other night.
Then I come to the fifth matter, the effective management of our public debt. On this matter an uncommon lot of nonsense has been talked, none more so than about the conversion loan, and we heard some of it this afternoon. This was the greatest financial operation in Canada's economic history. It was a major anti-inflationary step, it removed a heavy pressure on the bond market and it nearly doubled the average length of our debt.
Suppose there had been no conversion loan. What would have been the pressures upon the capital market with this heavy debt maturing? If such pressures had been added to the pressures which actually did develop in 1959, the result might well have been chaos. History, I believe, will prove that the conversion loan of 1958 has been one of the most farsighted acts of financial statesmanship ever undertaken.
Last Thursday evening and again this afternoon the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River engaged in some agile dialectics about the net debt. How it has risen, he exclaims. But he really did not tell the whole story in connection with it. It is true, of course, that our total net debt has risen but so has our ability to pay. The fact is that our per capita debt today is $681 as opposed to $849 in 1950 or $701 in 1956, the last full year of Liberal administration. Was the hon. gentleman heard in protest in those earlier years about the size of our per capita debt?

The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell
Equally, what is not clear from what he said this afternoon is that our net debt as a percentage of the gross national product has declined. Back in 1950, in the heyday of Doug. Abbott, our net debt was 71 per cent of our gross national product. When the Liberals went out of power it was 36 per cent. Today it is 34.9 per cent, a lower figure than in any previous year except 1958. The best evidence of effective debt management is, first, that public holdings of dominion of Canada bonds are at the highest level in the last 10 years and, second, that public subscriptions for the last Canada savings bonds were the highest ever. The public of Canada, with their dollars, have voted for the debt management policy of the government.
And the high interest rates.

That is an increase of $611.5 million or about 88 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, the
Atlantic adjustment grants have been a major contribution of the government. The settlement of the university grants issue with the province of Quebec on a mutually satisfactory


basis is a magnificent contribution to national unity. It is one for which credit must go to our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), to the Minister of Finance, to the late premier and the present premier of the province of Quebec. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The seventh major contribution of the government is its effective tariff policy. Attempts of a rather childish nature are made to claim that this government is a high protectionist government and has departed from the principles of multilateral trading. Since the government came to power there has been a firm adherence to the principles of the GATT. Indeed, what we have tried to do is to give leadership in GATT, not just pay lip service to it as our predecessors did. We have tried, with success, to use GATT as an instrument in the removal of restrictive trade practices, and this we must continue.
Let those who criticize our tariff policy assess the success of the negotiations regarding fruits and vegetables and textiles. Let our Liberal friends tell us during this debate if they would have ignored the tariff board report on fruits and vegetables. If not, will they not admit our genuine success in concluding these delicate negotiations with the United States? No constituency will profit more by that than the constituency of the hon. member for Essex East.
Before this debate is finished we shall probably hear much on textiles. That the Liberal party will seek to face both ways, I have no doubt. But this house knows and the country knows that the Liberal party wholly ignored the plight of the textile industry. It sold the industry down the river and it has not relented-

That is a specific and direct question that I put to him, and it should have a direct answer.
When do you want the answer?

My hon. friend
does not want an answer.

That is not true.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The amendments to the Customs Act which were so bitterly fought by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate (Mr. Pickersgill) and others have been a significant contribution to orderly trade. When he speaks perhaps the Leader of the Opposition would tell us directly whether the Liberal party would repeal them, amend them or retain them.
Coupled with this is my eighth point, namely effective leadership in commonwealth trade policy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my time is limited and I do not feel that I can accept questions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman leaves his point about textiles would he permit me to ask a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Normally I am most happy to answer questions, but my time is exceedingly limited and I am endeavouring to cover a very broad field.
In this area there is a significant difference between hon. gentlemen opposite and this government. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not really believe in commonwealth trade though they give lip service to it. We do believe in it and we do not apologize for this belief. As a direct result of the commonwealth trade conference, sterling and other European currencies have become convertible, a major advance, and the great majority of discriminatory restrictions against dollar imports have been eliminated.
What are the other results? Our contribution to the Colombo plan in southeast Asia was raised 50 per cent. For the first time we sponsored aid programs for the British West Indies and for Africa. This technical and other assistance was and is an act of enlightened leadership. I will admit that these are not the last word in aid to underdeveloped countries. Indeed we are probably but on the threshold. So long as people anywhere in the world are hungry this wealthy nation cannot be complacent. Well
The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell may it be that in this field will lie our greatest contribution to peace and the democratic way of life.
From the conference, as well, flowed the establishment of the commonwealth scholarship plan, a plan which in my view may prove ultimately to be a major beacon light of the 1950's.
I come to my ninth point, the major tax revisions. The replacement of the old dominion succession duty by the new Estate Tax Act was a major advance in tax legislation. But there have been other detailed and significant revisions of our tax structure. Take for example the new provision for a tax free gift of $10,000 between spouses respecting a jointly owned home, or in the case of a farm, between parent and child; the reduced sales tax on a wide range of municipal purchases; the inclusion of drugs, eyeglasses and many other categories in medical exemptions, as well as the raising of the exemption limits in this budget; the reduction in automobile excise tax; the very many tax reforms introduced, including in this budget two very significant proposals, first the relief from the impact of double taxation on pension benefits and, secondly, a new technique of tax deferment on profit sharing plans. Let it not be forgotten that for the lower and middle income groups income tax rates are lower than when this government was elected. The tax position of small corporations has also been greatly improved.
As my tenth point I wish to say a word about civil service matters. Controversy has obscured some of the major facts. Let me set the record straight. It was this government which put into effect the last civil service increase and which had to raise the funds for it. It was this government which proved itself the true friend of all civil servants by managing a change of government with the least upset of any change in Canadian history. There were literally no dismissals. Contrast that with the parade of firings which occurred when the Liberals came into power in 1935. What a scandalous and unconscionable display of political patronage occurred at that time including what Pierre Casgrain did in this very House of Commons, which was the worst of all.
It was this government which in its first year of office provided increases for superannuated civil servants, something which the former government for 10 years refused to do. It is this government which last session fully revised and improved the Defence Service Pension Act, the R.C.M.P. pension provisions and which at this session of parliament proposes a revision of the Public Service Superannuation Act. It is this government

The Budget-Mr. R.A. Bell which after Easter will introduce a complete revision and modernization of the Civil Service Act itself, to bring it up to date and to improve and assure for all time the true practice of the merit system.
It is this government which established the pay research bureau which the previous government had declined to do. It was established so that the pay data could be assembled on a scientific basis. This is the atmosphere in which the government at the first feasible opportunity had decided upon a class to class system of pay increases with increases for
50,000	civil servants effective at once and the balance before the end of summer. Oh, yes, I have neglected to mention the medical-surgical plan, one of the major advances in civil service matters.
Representing as I do more civil servants than perhaps any other hon. member of this house I am not unaware of the disappointment which existed at the decision not to approve a general pay increase last autumn. But I am satisfied that a class by class approach will enure in the very near future much more to the benefit of the average civil servant than a horizontal increase. We have seen how horizontal increases in freight rates have merely accentuated the existing discriminations. Continuous horizontal increases in salary perpetuate and intensify discriminations as between classes and help the high ranking civil servants to the detriment of the lower paid. That is why I believe this continuous class by class approach will prove much more effective and much more beneficial to those I represent than would a single horizontal increase. Under this approach, with the pay research bureau in action, review of salaries will be more regular, less discriminatory and more in the interests of the average civil servant. To my civil service friends in Carleton who have maintained a responsible and dignified attitude throughout this salary controversy I say-"give this new approach a real trial these next few months. I do not believe you will be disappointed."
I have taken the time to mention but 10 of the major accomplishments of a fiscal nature of this government but there are many others. If time permitted me to do so I would go on to enumerate them. I say, however, that this is a proud record of fiscal accomplishment. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) may justifiably take genuine satisfaction in the economic leadership they have given this country. The promotion of confidence in Canada's economic future, the encouragement and continuation of our unprecedented economic expansion, a continued

assault upon inflation, the maintenance of a sound dollar, the relief of the capital market thereby easing credit; these have been major objectives of this budget. These objectives have been achieved in the budget for 1960, I believe. In my opinion, in their accomplishment the Minister of Finance has earned the gratitude of the house and the country.
Mr. Speaker, before the hon. gentleman resumes his seat would he permit me a question.
